grammar.title: The Alphabet & Sounds
grammar.lead: English uses the Latin alphabet: 26 letters that combine to spell every word. Knowing the letter names and their basic sounds lets you spell your name, read new words, and follow spelling out loud.

leadTr.uz: Ingliz tili lotin alifbosidan foydalanadi: har bir soʻzni hijjalaydigan 26 ta harf. Harf nomlari va ularning tovushlarini bilish ismingizni hijjalash, yangi soʻzlarni oʻqish va ovozli hijjalashni tushunish imkonini beradi.
leadTr.ru: Английский использует латинский алфавит: 26 букв, из которых складывается каждое слово. Знание названий букв и их звуков помогает произносить по буквам своё имя, читать новые слова и понимать устное написание.

grammar.situation: You meet someone new: “What’s your name?” — “Anna.” — “How do you spell it?” — “A-N-N-A.” We spell words and names letter by letter, so knowing the letter names is the first step in English.

p: There are 26 letters. Five of them are vowels: A, E, I, O, U. The other 21 are consonants (B, C, D, F, G, …).
Sometimes Y acts like a vowel, as in happy or my.
ex: Vowels: A E I O U
Consonants: B C D F G H J K L M N P Q R S T V W X Y Z

p: Every letter has a name (how you say the letter) and a sound (how it works inside a word).
For example, the letter B is called “bee”, but its sound is /b/ as in book.
ex: C = “see” → sound /k/ in cat
H = “aitch” → sound /h/ in hat

p: We spell a word by saying each letter. Two of the same letter together are called “double”.
‘Hello’ = H – E – double L – O.
ex: “How do you spell cat?” — “C–A–T.”
‘Coffee’ = C–O–double F–double E… (F–F, E–E)

p: Each letter has a capital (A, B, C) and a small form (a, b, c).
We use capitals to start a sentence, for names, for the word I, and for countries, days and months.
ex: I live in Tashkent.
Monday, July, Anna

grammar.tip: Be careful with vowels — the same vowel can sound different: the a in cat is not the a in car. Listen and repeat new words to learn their real sound.
examples: B-O-O-K spells the word ‘book’.
‘Class’ has a double S: C-L-A-S-S.
My name is Anna — names start with a capital letter.
‘Hour’ begins with a silent H, so we say it like ‘our’.
The vowels in ‘education’ are e, a, i and o.
We say the letter W as ‘double-u’.

mistakes.x: My name is spelt with double “n”: N-N. (said as “en en”)
mistakes.v: Say each letter clearly: “double N”. English speakers often say “double” for two of the same letter.
In English the letter “i” is named /aɪ/ (“eye”), not /iː/.

quiz.q: Which of these is a vowel?
quiz.e: The vowels are A, E, I, O, U — so E is a vowel.

quiz.q: How many letters are in the English alphabet?
How do you spell 'dog'?
Which letter is a consonant?
quiz.e: M is a consonant; A, O and U are vowels.

quiz.q: The word 'sun' has how many letters?
The 'LL' in 'ball' is called ___.
quiz.e: Two of the same letter together are called ‘double’.

quiz.q: Which word begins with a vowel sound?
Choose the correct spelling.
Which word must start with a capital letter?
quiz.e: Names of cities (Tashkent) always take a capital letter.

quiz.q: 'Coffee' is spelled with ___.
quiz.e: C-O-F-F-E-E has double F and double E.

quiz.q: Which letter can act as a vowel in 'my'?
quiz.e: In ‘my’, Y works as a vowel.

quiz.q: How do you spell 'school'?
quiz.e: ‘School’ is S-C-H-O-O-L, with a silent H and double O.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses capitals correctly?
quiz.e: Capital I, capital for the city London, and a capital to start the sentence.

quiz.q: The name of the letter 'H' is ___.
Which word has a silent letter?
quiz.e: In ‘know’, the K is silent — we say /noʊ/.

grammar.title: Verb to be
grammar.lead: ‘Be’ is the most important verb in English. We use it to say who we are, how we feel, where things are, and to describe people and objects. It has three present forms: am, is, are.

leadTr.uz: ‘Be’ — ingliz tilidagi eng muhim feʼl. U kimligimizni, qanday his qilishimizni, narsalar qayerdaligini aytadi va taʼriflaydi. Hozirgi zamonda uch shakli bor: am, is, are.
leadTr.ru: ‘Be’ — важнейший глагол в английском. Им говорят, кто мы, как себя чувствуем, где находятся вещи, и описывают людей и предметы. В настоящем времени три формы: am, is, are.

grammar.situation: “I am a teacher. My sister is a doctor. We are from Tashkent.” The verb be connects a person to a job, a place or a description.

p: Use am with I, is with he / she / it, and are with you / we / they.
ex: I am a student. · She is happy. · They are at home.

p: In speaking and informal writing we join the pronoun and ‘be’: I’m, you’re, he’s, she’s, it’s, we’re, they’re.
ex: I’m tired. · He’s from Italy. · They’re teachers.

p: Add not after ‘be’. Short forms: isn’t (= is not), aren’t (= are not). ‘am not’ has no short form.
ex: She is not / isn’t here. · We are not / aren’t ready. · I am not cold.

p: To make a question, put ‘be’ before the subject. For wh‑questions, the wh‑word goes first.
ex: Are you a student? — Yes, I am. / No, I’m not.
Where is she? — She’s at school.

grammar.tip: Don’t confuse it’s (= it is) with its (possessive). ‘It’s cold’ = it is cold. ‘The dog likes its food’ = the food belonging to it.
examples: I am from Spain. (I’m from Spain.)
She is a nurse. (She’s a nurse.)
They are in the garden. (They’re in the garden.)
Is he your brother? — Yes, he is.
We aren’t ready yet.
It’s a cold morning. (It is)

mistakes.v: I am a student. / She is a doctor. (don’t drop “be”)
He is happy. (he/she/it → is)
I agree with you. (“agree” is a verb — no “be”)

quiz.q: I ___ a student.
She ___ from Tashkent.
We ___ friends.
The short form of 'he is' is ___.
They ___ at home.
___ you a teacher?
quiz.e: With ‘you’ we use ‘are’, and it comes first in a question.

quiz.q: He ___ happy today.
Choose the correct negative: 'We ___ ready.'
'___ she your sister?' — 'Yes, she ___.'
quiz.e: Question ‘Is she…?’ and short answer ‘Yes, she is.’

quiz.q: It ___ a beautiful day.
Which sentence is correct?
quiz.e: ‘am not’ has no contraction; we say ‘I’m not’.

quiz.q: 'Where ___ your parents?'
Complete: 'My name ___ Anna and I ___ ten.'
Choose the correct short answer: 'Are they students?'
quiz.e: In short answers we don’t contract: ‘Yes, they are.’

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'She are my best friend.'
quiz.e: With ‘she’ we use ‘is’: She is my best friend.

grammar.title: Pronouns & possessives
grammar.lead: Pronouns replace nouns so we don’t repeat names. Possessive words show who something belongs to. Getting these right makes your English sound natural.

leadTr.uz: Olmoshlar otlar oʻrnini bosadi, shunda ismlarni takrorlamaymiz. Egalik soʻzlari nimanidir kimga tegishliligini koʻrsatadi. Ularni toʻgʻri ishlatish nutqingizni tabiiy qiladi.
leadTr.ru: Местоимения заменяют существительные, чтобы не повторять имена. Притяжательные слова показывают принадлежность. Их правильное употребление делает речь естественной.

p: These do the action and usually come before the verb: I, you, he, she, it, we, they.
ex: He plays football. · We live here.

p: These receive the action and come after the verb or a preposition: me, you, him, her, it, us, them.
ex: She loves me. · Give the book to him. · I can see them.

p: These go before a noun to show owner: my, your, his, her, its, our, their.
ex: This is my bag. · Their house is big.

p: Possessive pronouns stand alone: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. We also add ’s to a name to show belonging.
ex: This book is mine. · That’s Anna’s pen (= the pen of Anna).

grammar.tip: ‘Their’ (owner), ‘there’ (place) and ‘they’re’ (= they are) sound the same but are different words. ‘Their car is over there, and they’re late.’
examples: This is my book and that one is yours.
Can you help me, please?
We like them, and they like us.
Her bag is blue; his is black.
That car is ours, not theirs.
This is Tom’s pen (the pen of Tom).

mistakes.v: I like coffee. (subject = I)
This is my book. (possessive = my)
She is my sister. (subject = she)

quiz.q: ___ play tennis every Sunday. (the speaker + friends)
quiz.e: Subject pronoun for the group with the speaker is ‘We’.

quiz.q: This is ___ book. (it belongs to me)
quiz.e: Before a noun we use the possessive adjective ‘my’.

quiz.q: I can see ___. (he)
quiz.e: After the verb we use the object pronoun ‘him’.

quiz.q: That car is ___. (it belongs to us)
quiz.e: Standing alone, we use the possessive pronoun ‘ours’.

quiz.q: ___ is a doctor. (female)
quiz.e: Subject pronoun for a female is ‘She’.

quiz.q: The dog likes ___ food. (belonging to the dog)
Give the keys to ___. (we)
quiz.e: After a preposition we use the object pronoun ‘us’.

quiz.q: This pen is ___. (it belongs to you)
quiz.e: Standing alone we use the possessive pronoun ‘yours’.

quiz.q: ___ parents are very kind. (they)
Whose bag is this? It's ___.
quiz.e: We add ’s to show possession: Anna’s.

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.e: The subject is ‘I’: I like coffee.

quiz.q: Complete: 'She gave ___ book to ___.'
Which uses 'theirs' correctly?
quiz.e: ‘theirs’ stands alone: This house is theirs.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'Its a beautiful day.'
quiz.e: Here we need ‘It’s’ (= it is), not the possessive ‘its’.

quiz.q: Complete: 'My brother and ___ are at school.' (I)
quiz.e: As part of the subject we use ‘I’: My brother and I.

grammar.title: Articles & nouns
grammar.lead: Articles (a, an, the) are small words before nouns. Choosing the right one — and knowing how to make plurals — is essential for clear, correct English.

leadTr.uz: Artikllar (a, an, the) ot oldidagi kichik soʻzlar. Toʻgʻrisini tanlash va koʻplik yasashni bilish aniq va toʻgʻri ingliz tili uchun zarur.
leadTr.ru: Артикли (a, an, the) — маленькие слова перед существительным. Правильный выбор и умение образовывать множественное число важны для грамотного английского.

p: Use a before a consonant sound and an before a vowel sound. We use them for singular things mentioned for the first time.
ex: a book · a university (‘yoo’ sound)
an apple · an hour (silent h)

p: Use the when both speaker and listener know which one, or there is only one.
ex: I bought a cake. The cake is delicious.
The sun is hot.

p: Most nouns add -s. After -s, -ss, -ch, -sh, -x we add -es. A consonant + y becomes -ies.
ex: book → books · box → boxes · baby → babies

p: Some plurals are irregular. Some nouns are uncountable (no plural, no a/an): water, rice, money, information.
ex: man → men · woman → women · child → children · foot → feet
I need some water (not ‘a water’).

grammar.tip: Choose a/an by the sound, not the letter. ‘an MP’ (em-sound) is correct; ‘a university’ (yoo-sound) is correct even though it starts with a vowel.
examples: I ate an apple and a banana.
There is a dog in the garden. The dog is friendly.
one box → two boxes; one baby → two babies.
The moon is bright tonight. (only one moon)
I need some water — not ‘a water’.
one child → three children (irregular).

mistakes.v: an apple / an hour (vowel sound)
I need information. (uncountable — no “a”, no “-s”)
She is a teacher. (jobs take “a/an”)

quiz.q: I have ___ apple.
quiz.e: ‘Apple’ starts with a vowel sound, so ‘an’.

quiz.q: She is reading ___ book.
quiz.e: ‘Book’ starts with a consonant sound, so ‘a’.

quiz.q: The plural of 'cat' is ___.
The plural of 'box' is ___.
___ sun is very bright today.
quiz.e: There is only one sun, so we use ‘the’.

quiz.q: The plural of 'baby' is ___.
I'd like ___ orange and ___ banana.
Which noun is uncountable?
quiz.e: ‘Water’ is uncountable — no plural, no a/an.

quiz.q: The plural of 'man' is ___.
I saw a film. ___ film was great.
quiz.e: The film is now known, so we use ‘the’.

quiz.q: Choose the correct article: '___ hour.'
quiz.e: ‘Hour’ has a silent h (vowel sound), so ‘an hour’.

quiz.q: Which is correct?
quiz.e: ‘University’ starts with a ‘yoo’ sound, so ‘a university’.

quiz.q: The plural of 'child' is ___.
Find the mistake: 'I need a money.'
quiz.e: ‘Money’ is uncountable: ‘I need money / some money.’

quiz.q: Complete: 'There is ___ egg and ___ spoon on ___ table.'

grammar.title: Demonstratives
grammar.lead: This, that, these and those point to people or things. They tell us about number (one or many) and distance (near or far).

leadTr.uz: This, that, these va those odam yoki narsalarga ishora qiladi. Ular son (bitta yoki koʻp) va masofani (yaqin yoki uzoq) bildiradi.
leadTr.ru: This, that, these и those указывают на людей или предметы. Они показывают число (один или много) и расстояние (близко или далеко).

p: Use this/these for things near you, and that/those for things far from you.
ex: This is my phone (in my hand). · That is your car (over there).

p: This and that are singular (one). These and those are plural (more than one).
ex: this book → these books
that shoe → those shoes

p: They can stand alone (a pronoun) or come before a noun (an adjective).
ex: This is delicious. (alone)
This cake is delicious. (+ noun)

p: We use them on the phone and to introduce people.
ex: Hello, this is Anna. (on the phone)
These are my friends, Tom and Sam.

grammar.tip: Match number carefully: ‘these book’ is wrong. Say this book (one) or these books (many).
examples: This phone (in my hand) is new.
That house (over there) is big.
These shoes are mine; those are yours.
Hello, this is Sara speaking. (on the phone)
These are my friends, Tom and Lucy.
That was a great film!

mistakes.v: this book (one) · these books (more than one)
I like those. (far = that/those)

quiz.q: ___ is my pen. (in my hand)
___ are my shoes. (near me)
Look at ___ bird in the sky. (far)
___ houses over there are new. (far)
The plural of 'this' is ___.
___ apples here are fresh.
Choose: 'Is ___ your bag?' (the one near you)
On the phone: 'Hello, ___ is Sara.'
quiz.e: We say ‘this is …’ to introduce ourselves on the phone.

quiz.q: The plural of 'that' is ___.
___ are my parents. (introducing them)
Which sentence is correct?
Complete: '___ shoes are nicer than ___ ones over there.'
Find the mistake: 'Look at those car near us.'
quiz.e: ‘car’ is singular and near, so ‘this car’ (or far ‘that car’).

quiz.q: Choose the natural sentence.
'___ is delicious!' (the cake you are eating now)

grammar.title: Present simple
grammar.lead: The present simple is the tense for facts, routines and habits — things that are generally true or happen regularly. It is the most common tense in everyday English.

leadTr.uz: Hozirgi oddiy zamon — faktlar, kundalik ishlar va odatlar uchun. U kundalik ingliz tilidagi eng koʻp ishlatiladigan zamon.
leadTr.ru: Present simple — для фактов, распорядка и привычек, того, что обычно верно или происходит регулярно. Это самое частое время в повседневном английском.

grammar.situation: Tom is a nurse. He works at a hospital. He starts at 8 and finishes at 4. He doesn’t work on Sundays. — Use the present simple for habits, routines and things that are generally true.

p: For routines (every day), facts (always true) and habits.
ex: I get up at seven every day.
Water boils at 100°C.

p: With he, she, it we add -s to the verb. After -o, -ss, -ch, -sh, -x we add -es; consonant + y → -ies.
ex: I work → she works · go → goes · study → studies

p: Use don’t (I/you/we/they) and doesn’t (he/she/it) + the base verb (no -s).
ex: They don’t eat meat. · He doesn’t like tea.

p: Use Do/Does + subject + base verb. Adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, never) go before the main verb.
ex: Do you play chess? · Does she work here?
I always brush my teeth.

grammar.tip: After does/doesn’t, the verb has no -s: ‘She doesn’t likes’ is wrong → ‘She doesn’t like.’ The -s is already in ‘does’.
examples: I get up at seven every day.
She goes to work by bus. (he/she/it + -s)
They don’t eat meat.
He doesn’t like coffee.
Do you play tennis? — Yes, I do.
We always have dinner at eight.

mistakes.v: He works in a bank. (he/she/it → add -s)
She doesn’t like tea. (he/she/it → doesn’t)
Do you like football? (after do/does, no -s)

quiz.q: He ___ to school every day.
I ___ coffee every morning.
quiz.e: With ‘I’ we use the base verb: drink.

quiz.q: They ___ football on Sundays.
quiz.e: With ‘they’ we use the base verb: play.

quiz.q: She ___ English very well.
We ___ in Tashkent.
quiz.e: With ‘we’ we use the base verb: live.

quiz.q: She ___ like fish.
The third-person form of 'study' is ___.
___ you like music?
Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.e: The frequency adverb goes before the verb: I always eat.

quiz.q: ___ she work on Saturdays?
Negative of 'He plays tennis': ___
quiz.e: doesn’t + base verb (no -s): He doesn’t play.

quiz.q: The third-person form of 'go' is ___.
Find the mistake: 'Does she likes pizza?'
quiz.e: After ‘does’ the verb has no -s: ‘Does she like pizza?’

quiz.q: Complete: 'My father ___ to work by bus, but I ___ to walk.'
Which is correct?
quiz.e: ‘never’ is already negative and goes before the verb: He never eats meat.

grammar.title: Present continuous
grammar.lead: The present continuous describes actions happening now, at this moment, or around now (a temporary situation). It is formed with ‘be’ + verb-ing.

leadTr.uz: Hozirgi davom zamoni hozir, shu daqiqada yoki shu atrofda (vaqtinchalik holat) sodir boʻlayotgan ishni bildiradi. ‘be’ + feʼl-ing bilan yasaladi.
leadTr.ru: Present continuous описывает действие, происходящее сейчас, в этот момент или в этот период (временно). Образуется ‘be’ + глагол-ing.

grammar.situation: Look! It is raining and the children are playing inside. — Use the present continuous for an action happening now, at the moment of speaking.

p: Use the right form of ‘be’ and add -ing to the main verb.
ex: I am reading. · She is sleeping. · They are playing.

p: Drop a final silent -e (make → making). Double the final consonant after a short stressed vowel (run → running). ‘ie’ → ‘y’ (lie → lying).
ex: write → writing · sit → sitting · die → dying

p: Present simple = routines/facts. Present continuous = happening now or temporary.
ex: I work in a bank. (job) — I’m working from home today. (now)

p: Negative: add not after ‘be’. Question: put ‘be’ first.
ex: She isn’t listening. · Are you working?

grammar.tip: Some verbs (like, want, know, love, need, understand) describe states, not actions. We don’t usually use them in the continuous: say ‘I want tea’, not ‘I am wanting tea’.
examples: Listen! The baby is crying.
I ’m reading a book right now.
They are playing in the park at the moment.
She isn’t working today.
Are you watching TV?
write → writing; run → running; lie → lying.

mistakes.x: I am go to school now.
mistakes.v: I am going to school now. (be + -ing)
She is cooking dinner. (don’t drop “is”)
I know the answer. (state verbs: no -ing)

quiz.q: Look! The baby ___ now.
They ___ in the garden at the moment.
I ___ a book right now.
The -ing form of 'make' is ___.
She ___ to music now.
The -ing form of 'run' is ___.
quiz.e: Short stressed vowel → double the consonant: running.

quiz.q: We ___ dinner at the moment.
Choose the 'now' sentence.
Negative: 'He ___ TV now.'
The -ing form of 'sit' is ___.
Which sentence is correct?
quiz.e: ‘want’ is a state verb — not used in the continuous: I want a coffee.

quiz.q: Complete: 'Be quiet! The students ___ a test.'
The -ing form of 'lie' is ___.
Choose the correct question.
Find the mistake: 'She is read a book now.'
quiz.e: After ‘is’ we need the -ing form: She is reading.

grammar.title: Have got · there is/are
grammar.lead: ‘Have got’ talks about possession, family and features. ‘There is / there are’ says that something exists or is present. Both are very common in everyday speech.

leadTr.uz: ‘Have got’ egalik, oila va xususiyatlar haqida. ‘There is / there are’ nimadir mavjudligini yoki borligini bildiradi. Ikkalasi ham kundalik nutqda juda koʻp uchraydi.
leadTr.ru: ‘Have got’ — о принадлежности, семье и признаках. ‘There is / there are’ — о существовании или наличии. Оба очень частотны в речи.

p: Use have got (I/you/we/they) and has got (he/she/it). Short forms: I’ve got, she’s got.
ex: I’ve got two brothers. · She’s got a new phone.

p: Negative: haven’t/hasn’t got. Question: Have/Has + subject + got?
ex: We haven’t got a car. · Has he got a sister?

p: Use there is (+ singular / uncountable) and there are (+ plural) to say something exists.
ex: There is a book on the table. · There are five chairs.

p: Negative: there isn’t / there aren’t. Question: Is there…? / Are there…?
ex: There isn’t any milk. · Are there any shops near here?

grammar.tip: Don’t mix them up: use have got for an owner (‘I have got a dog’) and there is/are for existence (‘There is a dog in the garden’).
examples: I ’ve got two sisters.
She ’s got a new phone.
We haven’t got a car.
Has he got a bike?
There is a book on the desk.
There are five chairs in the room.

mistakes.v: There are three rooms. (plural → there are)
She has got a car. (he/she/it → has got)

mistakes.x: I have got not a pen.
mistakes.v: I haven’t got a pen.

quiz.q: I ___ a new bag.
She ___ two cats.
___ a pen on the desk.
___ three windows in the room.
Short form of 'I have got' is ___.
We ___ a garden.
___ any milk in the fridge?
___ he got a bicycle?
quiz.e: With ‘he’ the question is ‘Has he got…?’.

quiz.q: There ___ a lot of people here.
Choose the correct negative: 'There ___ any chairs.'
Which sentence is correct?
quiz.e: With ‘she’: She has got a dog.

quiz.q: Complete: '___ a problem, but ___ no easy answers.'
Find the mistake: 'There is five students in the class.'
Which question is correct?
quiz.e: With ‘you’: Have you got a car?

quiz.q: Complete: 'My sister ___ long hair, and ___ a beautiful park near her house.'
quiz.e: ‘sister has got’ (possession) + ‘there is a park’ (existence, singular).

grammar.title: Modals: can/can't · imperatives
grammar.lead: ‘Can’ expresses ability, possibility and permission. ‘Can’t’ is its negative. The imperative gives instructions, orders and advice. Both are short and very useful.

leadTr.uz: ‘Can’ qobiliyat, imkoniyat va ruxsatni bildiradi. ‘Can’t’ uning inkori. Buyruq mayli koʻrsatma, buyruq va maslahat beradi. Ikkalasi ham qisqa va juda foydali.
leadTr.ru: ‘Can’ выражает способность, возможность и разрешение. ‘Can’t’ — его отрицание. Повелительное наклонение даёт указания, приказы и советы. Оба коротки и полезны.

grammar.situation: “Can you swim?” — “Yes, I can, but I can’t dive.” Can shows ability and possibility, and it never changes form.

p: Can + base verb means ‘is able to’. It never changes form (no -s, no ‘to’).
ex: I can swim. · She can speak three languages.

p: We also use can to ask for and give permission.
ex: Can I open the window? · You can go now.

p: The negative is can’t (cannot). Same form for all subjects.
ex: He can’t drive. · We can’t hear you.

p: Use the base verb to give an instruction. Add don’t for negative imperatives. We often add ‘please’ to be polite.
ex: Open your books. · Don’t run! · Please sit down.

grammar.tip: After ‘can’ never use ‘to’: ‘I can to swim’ is wrong → ‘I can swim.’ And ‘can’ has no -s with he/she/it: ‘She can swim’, not ‘She cans’.
examples: I can swim, but I can’t drive.
Can I open the window, please?
She can speak three languages.
Open your books. (instruction)
Don’t run in the corridor!
Please sit down.

mistakes.v: I can swim. (can + base verb, no “to”)
He can drive. (no -s on modals)
Please sit down. (imperative = base verb)

quiz.q: I ___ swim very well.
He ___ drive. He has no licence.
___ I borrow your pen?
___ your books, please. (instruction)
quiz.e: Imperative uses the base verb: Open.

quiz.q: She ___ speak French.
Negative imperative: '___ late!'
We ___ hear the teacher. It's too noisy.
Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.e: can + base verb: I can play.

quiz.q: '___ quiet, please.' (instruction)
They ___ come to the party. They're busy.
Which is correct?
quiz.e: ‘can’ takes no -s and the verb stays base: She can cook.

quiz.q: Make it negative: 'Touch the wall.'
Find the mistake: 'Can you to help me?'
quiz.e: After ‘can’ we don’t use ‘to’: Can you help me?

quiz.q: Complete: 'You ___ smoke here, but you ___ sit outside.'
Which gives polite advice correctly?

grammar.title: Adjectives
grammar.lead: Adjectives describe nouns — they tell us what people, places and things are like. Knowing where to put them and learning common opposites makes your descriptions clear.

leadTr.uz: Sifatlar otlarni taʼriflaydi — odam, joy va narsalar qanaqaligini aytadi. Ularning oʻrnini va keng tarqalgan qarama-qarshilarini bilish taʼrifni aniq qiladi.
leadTr.ru: Прилагательные описывают существительные — какими являются люди, места и вещи. Знание их места и распространённых антонимов делает описание ясным.

p: An adjective usually goes before the noun, or after the verb ‘be’. It never changes for plural.
ex: a red car · The car is red. · two red cars (not ‘reds’)

p: Learn adjectives in pairs.
ex: big ↔ small · hot ↔ cold · old ↔ new/young · happy ↔ sad · easy ↔ difficult

p: When two adjectives describe a noun, opinion comes before fact: a nice big house (opinion + size).
ex: a beautiful old city · a small black bag

p: Use very or really before an adjective to make it stronger.
ex: It’s very cold. · She’s really kind.

grammar.tip: Adjectives never take a plural -s in English: say ‘three big dogs’, not ‘three bigs dogs’.
examples: a red car → two red cars (never ‘reds’)
The flowers are beautiful.
big ↔ small · hot ↔ cold · easy ↔ difficult
a small black bag (size before colour)
It’s very cold today.
a nice big house (opinion before size)

mistakes.v: a red car (adjective before the noun)
They are happy. (adjectives have no plural -s)

quiz.q: Choose the correct order.
quiz.e: Adjective before noun: a red car.

quiz.q: The opposite of 'big' is ___.
The flowers are ___.
quiz.e: Adjective after ‘be’, no plural -s: are beautiful.

quiz.q: The opposite of 'hot' is ___.
It's a ___ day.
quiz.e: We need an adjective before ‘day’: a sunny day.

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence.
The opposite of 'difficult' is ___.
Which order is correct?
quiz.e: Size before colour: a small black bag.

quiz.q: She has ___ eyes.
Make it stronger: 'The film was ___ good.'
Find the mistake: 'I have two reds pens.'
quiz.e: Adjectives don’t take -s: two red pens.

quiz.q: Choose the natural order.
quiz.e: Opinion (nice) before size (big): a nice big house.

quiz.q: Complete: 'My grandfather is ___, but he feels ___.'
Which sentence is correct?
quiz.e: ‘interesting’ starts with a vowel sound → ‘an’, and the adjective goes before the noun.

quiz.q: Choose the correct description.
quiz.e: ‘an’ (vowel sound) + opinion/fact order: an expensive new phone.

grammar.title: Quantity: some / any
grammar.lead: ‘Some’ and ‘any’ talk about an amount that isn’t exact. Choosing between them depends on whether the sentence is positive, negative or a question — and on whether the noun can be counted.

leadTr.uz: ‘Some’ va ‘any’ aniq boʻlmagan miqdor haqida. Ular orasida tanlash gap tasdiq, inkor yoki savol ekanligiga va ot sanaladimi-yoʻqligiga bogʻliq.
leadTr.ru: ‘Some’ и ‘any’ говорят о неточном количестве. Выбор зависит от того, утверждение это, отрицание или вопрос, и можно ли сосчитать существительное.

p: Countable nouns have a plural (apple → apples). Uncountable nouns don’t (water, rice, money, bread).
ex: three apples (countable) · some water (uncountable)

p: Use some in affirmative sentences with plural and uncountable nouns.
ex: I have some friends here. · There is some milk in the cup.

p: Use any in negatives and most questions.
ex: I don’t have any money. · Is there any sugar?

p: We use some (not any) in polite offers and requests, even though they are questions.
ex: Would you like some tea? · Can I have some water, please?

grammar.tip: With uncountable nouns, don’t use a/an or a plural: say ‘some bread’, not ‘a bread’ or ‘breads’.
examples: I have some apples.
There isn’t any milk.
Is there any bread?
Would you like some tea? (offer)
Can I have some water? (request)
We have some rice but we don’t have any eggs.

mistakes.v: I don’t have any sugar. (negative → any)
Do you have any questions? (question → any)

quiz.q: I have ___ apples.
There isn't ___ juice.
Is there ___ bread?
Which noun is uncountable?
We have ___ eggs in the fridge.
Would you like ___ coffee?
He doesn't have ___ brothers.
Can I have ___ water, please?
Choose the correct sentence.
There are ___ books on the shelf.
Find the mistake: 'Do you have some questions?'
quiz.e: In a normal question we use ‘any’: Do you have any questions?

quiz.q: Complete: 'We have ___ rice but we don't have ___ vegetables.'
quiz.e: Positive → some rice; negative → any vegetables.

quiz.q: Which is correct?
Choose the natural offer.
o: Do you want some help — yes or no?
quiz.e: Offers use ‘some’: Would you like some cake?

quiz.q: Complete: 'Is there ___ milk? — Yes, there's ___.'

grammar.title: Prepositions
grammar.lead: Prepositions are small words that show relationships of place and time. The most common are in, on, at, and a few movement words. Learn them in fixed phrases.

leadTr.uz: Predloglar joy va vaqt munosabatlarini koʻrsatadigan kichik soʻzlar. Eng koʻp uchraydiganlari in, on, at va bir nechta harakat soʻzlari. Ularni tayyor iboralarda oʻrganing.
leadTr.ru: Предлоги — маленькие слова, показывающие отношения места и времени. Самые частые — in, on, at и несколько слов движения. Учите их в устойчивых выражениях.

p: in = inside / areas (in a box, in Tashkent). on = a surface (on the table, on the wall). at = a point/place (at the door, at school).
ex: The keys are in my bag. · The photo is on the wall. · I’m at home.

p: under (below), next to (beside), between (in the middle of two), behind, in front of, near.
ex: The cat is under the chair. · The bank is next to the school.

p: at + clock time/night (at 7, at night). on + days/dates (on Monday). in + months/years/parts of day (in July, in the morning).
ex: at 6 o’clock · on Friday · in 2026 · in the evening

p: Some phrases must be memorised.
ex: at home · at school · at work · in bed · on time · at the weekend

grammar.tip: Time prepositions follow a pattern: at = small (clock time), on = medium (a day), in = large (month/year). Think small → big.
examples: The book is on the table.
I live in Manchester.
The cat is under the chair.
We meet on Monday at 8 o’clock.
My birthday is in July.
The shop is between the bank and the café.

mistakes.v: I get up at 7 o’clock. (clock time → at)
See you on Monday. (days → on)

quiz.q: The book is ___ the table.
I live ___ Tashkent.
The cat is ___ the chair. (below it)
We meet ___ Monday.
School starts ___ 8 o'clock.
The shop is ___ the bank and the café.
quiz.e: In the middle of two things = between.

quiz.q: My birthday is ___ July.
She is ___ home now.
The picture is ___ the wall.
The dog is ___ the door, waiting.
Complete: 'I get up ___ 7 ___ the morning.'
quiz.e: Clock time ‘at 7’, part of day ‘in the morning’.

quiz.q: Which is correct?
Find the mistake: 'The bank is in front the school.'
o: in front the → in front of the
quiz.e: The phrase is ‘in front of’: in front of the school.

quiz.q: Complete: 'See you ___ the weekend, ___ Saturday ___ 5 pm.'
Choose the correct sentence.
o: The ball is on the box. (inside it)
The keys are in the table.
The lamp is between two windows.
quiz.e: ‘between two windows’ is correct; the others mix up in/on/at.

grammar.title: Question words
grammar.lead: Question words (wh- words) ask for information. Each one asks about something different — a person, a place, a time, a reason. Knowing them lets you ask about everything around you.

leadTr.uz: Savol soʻzlari (wh- soʻzlar) maʼlumot soʻraydi. Har biri boshqa narsani soʻraydi — odam, joy, vaqt, sabab. Ularni bilish atrofingizdagi hamma narsani soʻrash imkonini beradi.
leadTr.ru: Вопросительные слова (wh-) запрашивают информацию. Каждое спрашивает о своём — о человеке, месте, времени, причине. Зная их, вы можете спросить обо всём.

grammar.situation: “Where do you live?” “What do you do?” “When does the film start?” — Question words go first, then we use do / does + subject + verb.

p: What (thing), Who (person), Where (place), When (time), Why (reason), How (way/manner).
ex: What is this? · Who is she? · Where do you live? · Why are you late?

p: How many + countable (how many books). How much + uncountable / price (how much water, how much is it).
ex: How many students are there? · How much is this jacket?

p: wh- word + be + subject.
ex: Where is the station? · Who are they?

p: wh- word + do/does + subject + base verb.
ex: What do you want? · Where does she work?

grammar.tip: Use how many for things you can count and how much for things you can’t (and for prices): ‘How many apples?’ but ‘How much money?’
examples: What is your name?
Where do you live?
Who is that man?
When does the film start?
How many apples are there?
How much is this jacket?

mistakes.v: Where do you live? (add do/does)
What are you doing? (be questions: be + subject)
How much does it cost?

quiz.q: ___ is your name?
quiz.e: We ask about a name (thing) with ‘What’.

quiz.q: ___ do you live?
___ is your teacher?
___ is your birthday?
___ are you sad?
___ apples are there?
___ is this bag?
___ do you go to school?
___ old are you?
___ does she work?
Which question is correct?
quiz.e: wh- + be + subject: Where are you from?

quiz.q: Complete: '___ time ___ the film start?'
Find the mistake: 'How much books do you have?'
Choose the correct order.
quiz.e: wh- + do + subject + base verb: What do you want?

quiz.q: Complete: '___ is the weather today?'
quiz.e: We ask about weather with ‘How is the weather?’

grammar.title: Verb patterns: like + -ing
grammar.lead: To talk about activities you enjoy or dislike, English often uses a verb of feeling (like, love, hate, enjoy) followed by the -ing form. This is a key A1 pattern.

leadTr.uz: Yoqtirgan yoki yoqtirmagan mashgʻulotlar haqida gapirish uchun ingliz tili koʻpincha his feʼli (like, love, hate, enjoy) + -ing shaklini ishlatadi. Bu muhim A1 naqsh.
leadTr.ru: Чтобы говорить о занятиях, которые нравятся или нет, английский часто использует глагол чувства (like, love, hate, enjoy) + форму -ing. Это важная модель уровня A1.

p: After these verbs, an activity usually takes the -ing form.
ex: I like swimming. · She loves dancing. · They hate getting up early.

p: These verbs can also be followed directly by a noun.
ex: I like music. · She loves chocolate.

p: Use don’t/doesn’t + like/enjoy + -ing.
ex: I don’t like cooking. · He doesn’t enjoy running.

p: would like is different: it means ‘want’ and is followed by to + base verb or a noun.
ex: I’d like to go home. · I’d like a coffee.

grammar.tip: Don’t confuse like + -ing (enjoy an activity) with would like + to (want something now): ‘I like swimming’ vs. ‘I’d like to swim now.’
examples: I like swimming in summer.
She loves dancing.
They hate getting up early.
He doesn’t enjoy cooking.
I’d like to go home now. (= want)
I’d like a coffee, please.

mistakes.v: I like swimming. (like + -ing)
I enjoy reading. (enjoy + -ing)

quiz.q: I like ___ books.
She loves ___.
They hate ___ up early.
I like ___. (a noun)
We enjoy ___ football.
He doesn't like ___.
Choose the correct sentence.
She loves ___ to music.
I'd like ___ a sandwich, please.
quiz.e: would like + to + base verb: to have.

quiz.q: They don't enjoy ___ in winter.
Which sentence is correct?
quiz.e: would like + to + base verb: I’d like to swim.

quiz.q: Complete: 'She likes ___ but she'd like ___ a new hobby.'
Find the mistake: 'I love to cooking.'
quiz.e: After ‘love’ use -ing without ‘to’: I love cooking.

quiz.q: Choose the natural request.
o: I like to a tea, please.
quiz.e: Polite request: I’d like a tea, please.

quiz.q: Complete: 'Do you like ___? — Yes, but I'd like ___ a film tonight.'

grammar.title: Numbers & measures
grammar.lead: Numbers are everywhere — ages, prices, dates and the time. This lesson covers cardinal and ordinal numbers, and how to say dates, prices and the clock.

leadTr.uz: Sonlar hamma joyda — yosh, narx, sana va vaqt. Bu dars sanoq va tartib sonlarni, hamda sana, narx va soatni qanday aytishni oʻrgatadi.
leadTr.ru: Числа повсюду — возраст, цены, даты и время. Этот урок охватывает количественные и порядковые числительные, а также как называть даты, цены и время.

p: These count: one, two, three… Note the tricky ‘teens’ and ‘tens’: thirteen vs. thirty, fifteen vs. fifty.
ex: 13 = thirteen · 30 = thirty · 15 = fifteen · 50 = fifty

p: These show order: first (1st), second (2nd), third (3rd), fourth (4th)… We use them for dates and floors.
ex: the first of May · the third floor

p: Say the day as an ordinal: ‘the 5th of June’ or ‘June the 5th’. Years: 2026 = ‘twenty twenty-six’.
ex: My birthday is the 12th of July.

p: Prices: $5.50 = ‘five fifty’ / ‘five dollars fifty’. Time: 9:00 = ‘nine o’clock’, 9:15 = ‘quarter past nine’, 9:30 = ‘half past nine’, 9:45 = ‘quarter to ten’.
ex: It’s half past six. · It costs twenty euros.

grammar.tip: Listen for the stress to tell teens from tens: thirTEEN (stress at the end) vs. THIRty (stress at the start).
examples: 13 = thirteen; 30 = thirty.
the first of May; the third floor.
6:30 = half past six; 7:45 = quarter to eight.
It costs twenty pounds.
My exam is on the 12th of June.
2026 = ‘twenty twenty-six’.

mistakes.v: two hundred people (no -s after a number)
I am twenty years old.
It costs five dollars. (plural after numbers > 1)

quiz.q: How do you write the number 15?
The ordinal form of 'two' is ___.
Which is a month?
Which number comes after nineteen?
30 is written ___.
The 3rd of May means the ___ day of May.
The ordinal of 'five' is ___.

How do you say the year 2026?
Complete the date: 'My exam is on the ___ of March.' (1)
quiz.e: Dates use ordinals: the first of March.

quiz.q: It's 8:15. The correct phrase is ___.

reading.title: My Family
reading.text:
Hello! My name is Jack. I am eleven years old. I live in Manchester with my family.
I have one brother and one sister. My brother is fourteen and my sister is seven. My mother is a doctor and my father is a teacher.
We have a small dog. Its name is Bobby. Bobby is brown and very friendly. I love my family very much.

reading.title: Emily's Day
reading.text:
Emily is a student in Leeds. From Monday to Friday she gets up at seven o'clock. She has breakfast with her family and then goes to school by bus.
School starts at half past eight. Emily likes English and art, but she doesn't like maths.
In the afternoon she does her homework. In the evening she watches TV or reads a book. She goes to bed at ten o'clock.
At the weekend Emily doesn't go to school. She plays with her friends in the park.

quiz.e: She gets up at seven o’clock.

reading.title: At the Market
reading.text:
On Saturday morning, Tom and his mother go to the market in Oxford. The market is big and busy. There are many people and lots of fruit and vegetables.
Tom's mother wants to buy apples, bread and some milk. The apples are red and fresh. They cost two pounds for one kilo. Tom likes the oranges, so his mother buys four oranges too.
They don't buy any meat today because they have meat at home. After shopping, they are tired and thirsty, so they drink some water and go home by taxi.

quiz.q: Where do Tom and his mother go shopping?
quiz.e: They go to the market in Oxford.

quiz.e: She wants apples, bread and some milk.

quiz.q: How much do the apples cost?
quiz.e: The apples cost two pounds for one kilo.

reading.title: My Town
reading.text:
I live in a small town near Bath, in the west of England. It is a quiet place, but there is a lot to do.
In the centre there is a big park with tall trees and a small lake. Next to the park there is a library where I borrow books every week. There are two schools, a hospital and many shops.
My favourite place is the café on Green Street. It is between the post office and the bank. The coffee there is cheap and the people are friendly.
The town is not perfect — there isn't a cinema, and the buses are sometimes late. But I am happy here because my friends and family are close.

quiz.q: Where is the town?
quiz.e: It is a small town near Bath, in the west of England.

quiz.q: What is next to the park?
quiz.e: Next to the park there is a library.

quiz.q: Where is the writer's favourite café?
o: between the post office and the bank
quiz.e: The café is between the post office and the bank.

quiz.q: What does the town NOT have?
Why is the writer happy in the town?
o: because friends and family are close
quiz.e: He is happy because his friends and family are close.

reading.title: A Letter from Sophie
reading.text:
Dear Grace,

Thank you for your letter. I am very happy to hear from you. How are you and your family?

I am writing to you from my new home in Bristol. Last month we moved here from London because my father has a new job. At first I was sad because I missed my old friends, but now I feel better.

My new school is bigger than my old one. I am learning French and Spanish, and I really enjoy art. French is difficult, but my teacher is patient and I am getting better every day. After school I usually play netball with new friends.

Please write soon and tell me your news. Maybe you can visit me in the summer holidays!

Love,
Sophie

o: Her father got a new job.
quiz.e: They moved because her father has a new job.

quiz.q: How did Sophie feel at first?
quiz.e: At first she was sad because she missed her old friends.

quiz.q: How is her new school different?
quiz.e: Her new school is bigger than the old one.

quiz.q: What does Sophie say about French?
o: It is difficult, but she is improving.
quiz.e: French is difficult, but she is getting better, and her teacher is patient.

quiz.q: What does Sophie suggest Grace could do?
o: visit her in the summer holidays
quiz.e: She suggests Grace visit her in the summer holidays.

grammar.title: Past simple
grammar.lead: The past simple describes finished actions and states at a definite time in the past. It is the main tense for telling stories and talking about yesterday, last week, or years ago.
grammar.situation: “What did you do yesterday?” “I watched a film and went to bed early.” — Use the past simple for finished actions at a definite past time.

p: Most verbs add -ed. Verbs ending in -e add only -d; a consonant + y becomes -ied; a short stressed vowel doubles the final consonant.
ex: work → worked · live → lived · study → studied · stop → stopped

p: Many common verbs are irregular and must be learned.
ex: go → went · have → had · see → saw · make → made · buy → bought

p: Use didn’t + base verb for negatives, and Did + subject + base verb for questions. The main verb returns to its base form.
ex: I didn’t go out. · Did you see the film?

p: Past simple often appears with: yesterday, last night/week, two days ago, in 2010, when I was young.
ex: We arrived two hours ago. · She was born in 2009.

grammar.tip: After didn’t and did, never use the past form: ‘I didn’t went’ is wrong → ‘I didn’t go.’ The past is already shown by ‘did’.
examples: "Yesterday I watched a film and cooked dinner."
"She went to London last summer."
"They didn’t come to the party."
"Did you finish your homework? — Yes, I did."
"He bought a new bike two weeks ago."
"We were very tired after the trip."

mistakes.x: I goed home. / She buyed it.
mistakes.v: I went home. / She bought it. (irregular verbs)
Did you go there? (after did → base verb)
I didn’t see him.

quiz.q: Yesterday I ___ football with my friends.
The past simple of 'go' is ___.
She ___ a sandwich for lunch.
We ___ to the cinema last night.
The past simple of 'study' is ___.
I ___ TV yesterday evening.
They ___ come to school yesterday.
___ you see Tom last week?
The past simple of 'buy' is ___.

Find the mistake: 'I didn't went home.'
quiz.e: After ‘didn’t’ use the base verb: I didn’t go home.

quiz.q: Complete: 'She ___ a letter and ___ it to her friend.'
Which question is correct?
quiz.e: Did + base verb: Did you go out?

quiz.q: Complete: 'We ___ tired, so we ___ early.'
The past simple of 'can' is ___.

grammar.title: Past continuous
grammar.lead: The past continuous describes an action in progress at a moment in the past. It is often used to set the scene in a story, or for an action interrupted by another.
grammar.situation: “At 8 o’clock last night I was watching TV when the phone rang.” — The past continuous sets the longer background; the past simple is the shorter action that interrupts it.

p: Use was (I/he/she/it) or were (you/we/they) + verb-ing.
ex: I was reading. · They were playing outside.

p: Use past continuous for the longer action and past simple for the shorter one that interrupts it, often joined by when or while.
ex: I was sleeping when the phone rang.
While she was cooking, he arrived.

p: Use past continuous for two longer actions happening at the same time.
ex: I was reading while my brother was watching TV.

p: Negative: wasn’t/weren’t + -ing. Question: Was/Were + subject + -ing?
ex: She wasn’t listening. · Were you working at 8 pm?

grammar.tip: Use the past simple for the short, completed action and the past continuous for the longer background action: ‘I was walking home when it started to rain.’
examples: "At 8 o’clock last night I was studying."
"They were watching TV when I came in."
"While we were having dinner, the lights went out."
"She wasn’t sleeping at midnight."
"Were you waiting for me?"
"He fell while he was running."

mistakes.v: I was watching TV. (was/were + -ing)
While I was cooking, he arrived.

quiz.q: At 7 pm yesterday I ___ dinner.
They ___ football when it started to rain.
She ___ a book at 9 o'clock.
We ___ TV all evening.
The past continuous of 'he sleeps' is ___.
I ___ when the phone rang.
While she ___, he arrived.
They ___ when I called.
___ you sleeping at midnight?
Choose: 'I was walking home ___ it started to snow.'
Find the mistake: 'They was playing in the garden.'
Complete: 'While I ___ TV, my sister ___ her homework.'
quiz.e: Two parallel past actions → both continuous.

quiz.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: When I arrived, she was cooking.
When I was arriving, she cooked.
When I arrive, she was cooking.

quiz.q: Complete: 'What ___ you ___ at 10 pm?'
Choose the correct pair.
o: I was reading when he was calling.
I read when he was calling.
I was reading when he called.
I was read when he called.

grammar.title: Present perfect
grammar.lead: The present perfect links the past and the present. We use it for life experiences (without saying exactly when), recent actions with a present result, and situations that started in the past and continue now.
grammar.situation: “I have visited London twice.” We don’t say when — the experience matters now, not the exact time.

p: Use have (I/you/we/they) or has (he/she/it) + the past participle (the 3rd form: done, gone, seen, been).
ex: I have seen that film. · She has finished her work.

p: Use ever in questions and never in negatives to talk about experiences at any time in your life.
ex: Have you ever been to London? · I have never eaten sushi.

p: just = a very short time ago; already = sooner than expected; yet = used in questions and negatives at the end.
ex: I’ve just arrived. · She’s already left. · Have you finished yet?

p: Use for + a period of time and since + a point in time for situations continuing now.
ex: We’ve lived here for five years. · I’ve known him since 2018.

grammar.tip: Don’t use the present perfect with a finished past time. Say ‘I saw her yesterday’ (past simple), not ‘I have seen her yesterday’. Use the present perfect when the time is unfinished or unstated.
examples: "I have visited three countries."
"Have you ever ridden a horse?"
"She has never tried Italian food."
"We’ve just finished dinner."
"He has already done his homework."
"They’ve lived here for ten years."

mistakes.v: I saw him yesterday. (definite time → past simple)
She has gone home. (past participle)
I have been here since Monday.

quiz.q: I ___ my homework. (it's finished now)
She ___ to Paris. (experience)
The past participle of 'see' is ___.
We ___ this film before.
They ___ just arrived.
Have you ___ been to Spain?
quiz.e: In questions about experience we use ‘ever’.

quiz.q: I've ___ eaten octopus. (not in my life)
Has she finished ___?
quiz.e: In questions, ‘yet’ goes at the end.

quiz.q: We've lived here ___ 2015.
I've known him ___ ten years.
quiz.e: A period of time → for ten years.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'I have seen her yesterday.'
quiz.e: With ‘yesterday’ (finished time) use past simple: I saw her yesterday.

quiz.q: Complete: 'She ___ already ___ the email.'
Which is correct?
quiz.e: ‘yet’ goes at the end of the question.

quiz.q: Complete: 'I ___ this book ___ three days, but I haven't finished it.'
The past participle of 'go' (experience: visit and return) is ___.
quiz.e: For an experience there and back we use ‘been’: I have been to Rome.

grammar.title: Future: will & going to
grammar.lead: English has several ways to talk about the future. The two most common at A2 are ‘will’ and ‘be going to’. Each fits different situations — predictions, decisions, plans and intentions.

p: Use will + base verb for instant decisions, offers, promises and general predictions. Short form: ’ll; negative: won’t.
ex: I’ll help you. · It will rain tomorrow. · I won’t be late.

p: Use be going to + base verb for plans you have already decided and for predictions based on what you can see now.
ex: We’re going to visit Rome. · Look at the sky — it’s going to rain.

p: A decision made now = will; a plan decided before = going to.
ex: (phone rings) I’ll get it! · I’m going to study tonight. (already planned)

p: For fixed arrangements with a time, the present continuous is also common.
ex: I’m meeting Sara at six. · We’re flying on Monday.

grammar.tip: For a decision you make while speaking, use will: ‘I’ll have the chicken, please.’ For something you already planned, use going to: ‘I’m going to start a new job.’
examples: "I think it will be sunny tomorrow."
"Don’t worry, I ’ll carry that bag for you."
"We ’re going to buy a new car next month."
"Look out — you ’re going to drop it!"
"She won’t come to the meeting."
"I ’m meeting the doctor at 3 pm."

mistakes.v: I will call you. (will + base verb)

mistakes.x: Look at the clouds — it will rain.
mistakes.v: …it’s going to rain. (evidence now → going to)

quiz.q: I think it ___ rain tomorrow.
We ___ visit our grandparents next week. (a plan)
quiz.e: A decided plan → are going to visit.

quiz.q: The negative of 'will' is ___.
(The phone rings.) I ___ answer it!
quiz.e: An instant decision → I’ll answer it.

quiz.q: Look at those clouds! It ___ rain.
quiz.e: Prediction from evidence → is going to rain.

quiz.q: She ___ be twelve next month.
They ___ move to a new house. (already decided)
quiz.e: A plan → are going to move.

quiz.q: I promise I ___ tell anyone.
What ___ you ___ do at the weekend? (plans)
quiz.e: Asking about plans → are you going to do?

quiz.q: Choose the instant decision.
Find the mistake: 'I will to call you later.'
quiz.e: After ‘will’ use the base verb: I will call you.

quiz.q: Complete: 'A: I'm cold. B: I ___ close the window.'
quiz.e: Reacting now (offer) → I’ll close the window.

quiz.q: Which shows a fixed arrangement?
quiz.e: Arrangement with a time → present continuous.

quiz.q: Complete: 'We ___ (plan) start a business, and we hope it ___ (prediction) succeed.'
o: are going to / are going to
quiz.e: Plan → going to start; prediction → will succeed.

quiz.q: Choose the correct prediction from evidence.
o: She will have a baby — look!
She's going to have a baby — look!
She will to have a baby.
quiz.e: Evidence-based prediction → is going to have.

grammar.title: Comparatives & superlatives
grammar.lead: We use comparatives to compare two things and superlatives to compare one thing with all the others in a group. The form depends on the length of the adjective.

p: One-syllable adjectives: add -er (comparative) and -est (superlative). Double a final consonant after a short vowel; -y becomes -ier/-iest.
ex: tall → taller → the tallest · big → bigger · happy → happier

p: Two or more syllables: use more (comparative) and the most (superlative).
ex: expensive → more expensive → the most expensive

p: Use than after a comparative, and the before a superlative.
ex: She is taller than me. · It’s the biggest city in the country.

p: A few adjectives are irregular.
ex: good → better → the best · bad → worse → the worst · far → further

grammar.tip: Don’t mix the two forms: ‘more taller’ and ‘most biggest’ are wrong. Use either -er/-est or more/most, never both.
examples: "Today is hotter than yesterday."
"This is the cheapest phone in the shop."
"Maths is more difficult than art for me."
"She is the most intelligent student in the class."
"My new car is better than my old one."
"It was the worst film I’ve ever seen."

mistakes.x: She is more taller than me.
mistakes.v: She is taller than me. (don’t use “more” with -er)
It is the biggest. (short adjective → -est)
He is better. (irregular)

quiz.q: This box is ___ than that one.
He is the ___ boy in the class.
quiz.e: Superlative of a short adjective: the tallest.

quiz.q: A car is ___ than a bicycle.
The comparative of 'big' is ___.
Gold is ___ than silver.
This is the ___ restaurant in town.
Today is ___ than yesterday.
The superlative of 'happy' is ___.
She is ___ student in the school.
quiz.e: Long adjective superlative: the most intelligent.

quiz.q: My bag is ___ than yours.
Find the mistake: 'This is more cheaper than that.'
Complete: 'It is ___ city ___ the country.'
quiz.e: Superlative: the biggest city in the country.

quiz.q: Which is correct?
Complete: 'This exam was ___ than the last one, but not ___ I've ever taken.'
quiz.e: more difficult than … the most difficult.

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: My results are gooder than his.
My results are better than his.
My results are more good than his.
My results are best than his.

grammar.title: Adverbs of manner
grammar.lead: Adverbs of manner tell us how an action is done. They usually describe a verb and most are formed from adjectives.

p: Most adverbs add -ly to the adjective. Adjectives ending in -y change to -ily; -le changes to -ly.
ex: slow → slowly · happy → happily · simple → simply

p: Some adverbs are irregular or the same as the adjective.
ex: good → well · fast → fast · hard → hard · early → early

p: The adverb usually goes after the verb (or after the object).
ex: She sings beautifully. · He drives the car carefully.

p: An adjective describes a noun; an adverb describes a verb.
ex: He is a careful driver. (adjective) · He drives carefully. (adverb)

grammar.tip: ‘Good’ is an adjective; its adverb is well: ‘She is a good singer’ but ‘She sings well.’ ‘She sings good’ is wrong.
examples: "He speaks English fluently."
"Please drive slowly."
"She plays the piano well."
"They worked hard all day."
"The children played happily in the garden."
"He answered the question correctly."

mistakes.v: He speaks English very well. (good → well)
She sings beautifully. (verb → adverb)

quiz.q: She sings ___.
The adverb of 'quick' is ___.
He runs very ___.
quiz.e: ‘fast’ is the same as adverb and adjective.

quiz.q: Please speak ___.
The adverb of 'good' is ___.
They worked ___ all day.
quiz.e: ‘hard’ (= with effort) is the adverb; ‘hardly’ means ‘almost not’.

quiz.q: She plays the violin ___.
The adverb of 'happy' is ___.
He drives ___.
Choose the adverb sentence.
Find the mistake: 'He sings very good.'
quiz.e: Use the adverb ‘well’: He sings very well.

quiz.q: Complete: 'She is a ___ worker and she works ___.'
Which is correct?
quiz.e: Adverb after the object: answered the question correctly.

quiz.q: Complete: 'The test was ___, so she finished it ___.'
Choose the correct adverb form.

grammar.title: Quantifiers: much, many, a lot of
grammar.lead: Quantifiers say how much or how many. The right one depends on whether the noun is countable or uncountable, and whether the sentence is positive, negative or a question.

p: Use many with countable nouns and much with uncountable nouns, mostly in questions and negatives.
ex: How many apples? · How much water? · I don’t have much time.

p: Use a lot of (or lots of) with both countable and uncountable nouns, usually in positive sentences.
ex: She has a lot of friends. · We have a lot of homework.

p: Use a few with countable nouns and a little with uncountable nouns to mean ‘a small amount’.
ex: I have a few questions. · Add a little salt.

p: too much/many = more than you want; enough = the right amount.
ex: There are too many cars. · We don’t have enough chairs.

grammar.tip: In positive sentences, a lot of usually sounds better than ‘much’ or ‘many’: say ‘I have a lot of work’, not ‘I have much work’.
examples: "How many students are in your class?"
"There isn’t much milk left."
"We have a lot of homework today."
"I only need a few minutes."
"Add a little sugar to the tea."
"There are too many people here."

mistakes.v: How many books? (countable → many)
I have a lot of money. (uncountable, positive → a lot of)

quiz.q: How ___ apples do you want?
How ___ water is there?
She has ___ friends.
I have ___ books on this subject.
Add ___ salt to the soup.
There isn't ___ time left.
We don't have ___ chairs.
There are ___ people in the room. (more than we want)
I'd like ___ sugar in my coffee.
We have ___ homework tonight.
Find the mistake: 'I have much friends.'
quiz.e: Countable positive → ‘many’ or ‘a lot of’ friends.

quiz.q: Complete: 'There isn't ___ juice, but there are ___ apples.'
Which is correct?
o: We don't have a enough chairs.
quiz.e: ‘enough’ goes before the noun: enough chairs.

quiz.q: Complete: 'How ___ money do you need? Only ___.'
Choose the natural sentence.
o: He drinks a lot of coffee.
quiz.e: Positive + uncountable → a lot of coffee.

grammar.title: Verb + infinitive or -ing
grammar.lead: After certain verbs we use the infinitive (to + verb); after others we use the -ing form. Learning which verbs take which form is an important A2 skill.

p: These verbs are followed by to + base verb: want, would like, need, decide, hope, plan, promise, learn, try.
ex: I want to go home. · She decided to stay. · We hope to win.

p: These verbs are followed by the -ing form: like, love, enjoy, hate, finish, stop, mind, suggest, practise.
ex: I enjoy reading. · They finished eating. · Do you mind waiting?

p: Use to + verb to explain why you do something (the purpose).
ex: I went to the shop to buy milk.

p: like + -ing = enjoy in general; would like + to = want now.
ex: I like swimming. · I’d like to swim now.

grammar.tip: Memorise verbs in short phrases: ‘want to go’, ‘enjoy going’. When unsure, remember that want, need, hope and decide take to, while enjoy, finish and stop take -ing.
examples: "I want to learn Spanish."
"She enjoys cooking for her family."
"They decided to move to a new city."
"He finished doing his homework."
"We went out to celebrate her birthday."
"Do you mind opening the window?"

mistakes.v: I want to go home. (want + to)
I enjoy swimming. (enjoy + -ing)

quiz.q: I want ___ home.
She enjoys ___.
We hope ___ the match.
They finished ___ dinner.
I need ___ a doctor.
He decided ___ at home.
Do you mind ___ the door?
I went to the library ___ a book.
She stopped ___ because she was tired.
We learned ___ in summer.
Find the mistake: 'I enjoy to read books.'
Complete: 'She wants ___ a teacher, so she's learning ___ children.'
quiz.e: want + to (to become); learn + to (but here ‘teaching’ as a noun-like activity she practises) → best: to teach. (to become / to teach)

quiz.q: Which is correct?
quiz.e: would like + to: I’d like to swim.

quiz.q: Complete: 'He finished ___ and then decided ___ for a walk.'
Choose the purpose sentence.
o: I study to passing the exam.
I study to pass the exam.
I study for pass the exam.
quiz.e: Purpose uses to + base verb: to pass.

grammar.title: Present perfect vs past simple
grammar.lead: These two tenses both talk about the past, but they are used differently. The past simple is for a finished time; the present perfect connects the past to now.

p: Use the past simple with a finished time word (yesterday, last week, in 2010). Use the present perfect when the time is unstated or unfinished (today, this week, ever).
ex: I saw her yesterday. · I have seen that film. (when? not important)

p: Present perfect = experience at any time. Past simple = a specific completed event.
ex: Have you ever been to Rome? — Yes, I went there in 2019.

p: Present perfect shows a present result; past simple just reports a finished action.
ex: I’ve lost my keys. (I can’t find them now) · I lost my keys yesterday.

p: Past simple: yesterday, ago, last…, in 2015. Present perfect: ever, never, just, already, yet, recently, since, for.
ex: She moved here two years ago. · She has lived here for two years.

grammar.tip: A finished time word forces the past simple. ‘I have finished it yesterday’ is wrong → ‘I finished it yesterday.’
examples: "I have visited Paris, but I visited it last spring."
"She has just left."
"They arrived two hours ago."
"Have you ever eaten sushi? — Yes, I tried it in Tokyo."
"We have known each other since 2018."
"He didn’t call me yesterday."

mistakes.v: I finished it yesterday. (yesterday = finished time)
Have you ever eaten sushi? (life experience → present perfect)

quiz.q: I ___ my homework yesterday.
She ___ to Japan. (experience)
We ___ a great film last night.
He ___ his keys. (he can't find them now)
They ___ here in 2015.
___ you ever ___ a horse?
quiz.e: Experience question → Have you ever ridden?

quiz.q: I ___ him two days ago.
She's not here; she ___ already ___.
We ___ in this town for ten years.
quiz.e: ‘for ten years’ continuing → present perfect: have lived.

quiz.q: What time ___ you ___ home last night?
quiz.e: ‘last night’ → past simple: did you arrive?

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'I have seen her last week.'
quiz.e: ‘last week’ forces past simple: I saw her last week.

quiz.q: Complete: 'I ___ Tom for years. We ___ at school in 2010.'
Which is correct?
o: Did you ever go to Spain?
Have you ever been to Spain?
Have you ever went to Spain?
Did you ever been to Spain?

quiz.q: Complete: 'She ___ three books this year, and she ___ this one last weekend.'
Choose the sentence with a present result.
o: I've broken my arm — it hurts!
quiz.e: Present perfect shows the result now: I’ve broken my arm.

grammar.title: used to
grammar.lead: We use ‘used to’ to talk about past habits and states that are no longer true. It is a simple way to contrast the past with the present.
grammar.situation: “I used to play tennis, but I stopped years ago.” — used to describes a past habit or state that is no longer true.

p: used to + base verb describes something that happened regularly in the past, or a state that was true before but isn’t now.
ex: I used to play football every day. · She used to live in Leeds.

p: Negative: didn’t use to (no -d). Question: Did … use to…?
ex: He didn’t use to like coffee. · Did you use to have long hair?

p: ‘used to’ always contrasts the past with now.
ex: I used to smoke, but now I don’t. · We didn’t use to have a car, but now we do.

p: For present habits, use the present simple, not ‘used to’.
ex: Now I go to the gym every day. (not ‘I use to go’)

grammar.tip: In negatives and questions the ‘-d’ disappears: ‘didn’t use to’ and ‘Did you use to…?’, never ‘didn’t used to’.
examples: "I used to live in a small village."
"She used to have long hair."
"We didn’t use to watch much TV."
"Did you use to walk to school?"
"He used to be shy, but now he’s very confident."
"They used to play outside every afternoon."

mistakes.v: I used to live here. (affirmative: used)
I didn’t use to smoke. (after did → use, no -d)

quiz.q: I ___ play tennis when I was young.
She ___ live in London.
We ___ have a dog.
They ___ go to the beach every summer.
He ___ be very thin.
Negative: 'I ___ like vegetables.'
quiz.e: Negative drops the -d: didn’t use to.

quiz.q: ___ you use to have long hair?
She ___ like coffee, but now she loves it.
quiz.e: Negative past habit: didn’t use to.

quiz.q: We ___ play outside, but now we stay in.
Choose the correct question.
quiz.e: Did + use to (no -d): Did you use to smoke?

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'He didn't used to study hard.'
o: didn't used to → didn't use to
quiz.e: Drop the -d after didn’t: didn’t use to study.

quiz.q: Complete: 'I ___ be afraid of dogs, but now I ___ them.'
Which sentence is correct for a present habit?
o: Now I use to run daily.
Now I used to run daily.
Now I am use to run daily.
quiz.e: For present habits use the present simple: I run daily.

quiz.q: Complete: '___ they ___ live near here?'
quiz.e: Did + use to: Did they use to live…?

quiz.q: Choose the natural contrast.
o: I used to play piano, and I still do every day exactly the same.
I used to play piano, but I stopped years ago.
I use to play piano now.
I am used to play piano before.
quiz.e: ‘used to’ contrasts a past habit with the present (now stopped).

grammar.title: Obligation: must, have to, should
grammar.lead: These modal verbs talk about rules, necessity and advice. ‘Must’ and ‘have to’ express obligation; ‘should’ gives advice; their negatives have different meanings.

p: must and have to + base verb both mean something is necessary. ‘Must’ often comes from the speaker; ‘have to’ often comes from outside rules.
ex: You must wear a seatbelt. · I have to work on Saturday.

p: should + base verb gives advice or an opinion about the best thing to do.
ex: You should see a doctor. · We shouldn’t waste food.

p: mustn’t = it is prohibited (don’t do it!). don’t have to = it isn’t necessary (but you can).
ex: You mustn’t smoke here. (forbidden) · You don’t have to come. (optional)

p: The past of both ‘must’ and ‘have to’ is had to.
ex: Yesterday I had to stay late at work.

grammar.tip: Be careful: mustn’t and don’t have to are very different. ‘You mustn’t go’ = do NOT go. ‘You don’t have to go’ = you can stay if you like.
examples: "You must stop at a red light."
"I have to get up early tomorrow."
"You should drink more water."
"You mustn’t use your phone in the exam."
"We don’t have to pay — it’s free."
"She had to wait an hour for the bus."

mistakes.x: You mustn’t pay — it’s free, so it’s OK not to.
mistakes.v: You don’t have to pay. (no obligation ≠ mustn’t)
He must go. (must + base verb)

quiz.q: You ___ wear a uniform at this school. (rule)
You look tired. You ___ go to bed.
You ___ smoke here. It's forbidden.
I ___ get up early tomorrow.
We ___ waste water.
It's free, so you ___ pay.
Students ___ be quiet in the library. (rule)
The past of 'I must leave' is ___.
quiz.e: Past of must/have to → had to leave.

quiz.q: You're ill. You ___ see a doctor.
You ___ touch that — it's dangerous!
Find the difference: 'You don't have to come.' means ___.
Complete: 'You ___ be late, but you ___ come if you're busy.'
Which gives advice correctly?
quiz.e: should + base verb: You should study more.

quiz.q: Complete: 'Yesterday I ___ work late, so I ___ cancel my plans.'
Choose the prohibition.
o: You don't have to park here.

grammar.title: First conditional
grammar.lead: The first conditional talks about a real or likely situation in the future and its result. It uses ‘if’ + present simple for the condition and ‘will’ for the result.
grammar.situation: “If it rains tomorrow, we ’ll stay at home.” — The first conditional talks about a real, likely future result.

p: The if-clause uses the present simple; the result clause uses will + base verb.
ex: If it rains, we will stay home.
I will call you if I have time.

p: You can start with either clause. Use a comma only when the if-clause comes first.
ex: If you study, you’ll pass. · You’ll pass if you study.

p: unless means ‘if … not’.
ex: You’ll be late unless you hurry. (= if you don’t hurry)

blocks.h: may / might / can in the result
p: Instead of ‘will’, you can use may, might (possible) or can (ability) in the result.
ex: If it’s sunny, we might go to the beach.

grammar.tip: Don’t use ‘will’ in the if-clause: ‘If it will rain’ is wrong → ‘If it rains, we will stay home.’ The condition is in the present simple.
examples: "If it rains, we will stay at home."
"If you heat ice, it melts."
"I’ll help you if you ask me."
"You’ll miss the bus unless you run."
"If she studies hard, she will pass."
"If we leave now, we might catch the train."

mistakes.x: If it will rain, I will stay in.
mistakes.v: If it rains, I will stay in. (no “will” after if)

grammar.title: Relative clauses
grammar.lead: Relative clauses give extra information about a noun. They begin with a relative pronoun — who, which, that, where — and help you build longer, more natural sentences.

p: Use who for people and which for things and animals.
ex: The man who lives next door is a doctor.
I bought a phone which takes great photos.

p: that can replace who or which in many sentences, especially in speaking.
ex: The book that I read was excellent.

p: Use where to talk about a place.
ex: This is the café where we first met.

p: Use whose to show that something belongs to someone.
ex: That’s the girl whose brother is a singer.

grammar.tip: Use who for people, which for things; that can replace either. Don’t add an extra pronoun: ‘The man who he lives next door’ is wrong — drop ‘he’.
examples: "The woman who teaches us is very kind."
"This is the laptop which I bought yesterday."
"He’s the player that scored the goal."
"That’s the town where I was born."
"She’s the friend whose car we borrowed."
"The film that we saw was boring."

grammar.title: Linking words: because, so, but, although
grammar.lead: Linking words join ideas to make your writing and speaking flow. They show reasons, results, contrasts and additions between two parts of a sentence.

p: because introduces a reason; so introduces a result.
ex: I stayed home because I was ill. · I was ill, so I stayed home.

p: but joins two contrasting ideas in one sentence; however often starts a new sentence.
ex: It was cold, but we went out. · It was cold. However, we went out.

p: although introduces a surprising contrast within a sentence.
ex: Although it was raining, we played football.

p: and adds; or gives a choice; also adds extra information.
ex: We had tea and cake. · Tea or coffee? · She sings; she also dances.

grammar.tip: ‘because’ is followed by a reason and ‘so’ by a result. ‘I was tired because I worked late’ = the reason; ‘I worked late, so I was tired’ = the result.
examples: "I was hungry, so I made a sandwich."
"She passed because she studied hard."
"He’s rich, but he isn’t happy."
"Although she was tired, she finished the work."
"Would you like tea or coffee?"
"It rained all day, so we stayed inside."

mistakes.x: Although it was hard but he tried.

grammar.title: Question tags
grammar.lead: Question tags are short questions added to the end of a statement, used to check information or invite agreement. The tag matches the tense and reverses the verb.

p: After a positive statement, the tag is negative, using the same auxiliary verb.
ex: You’re from Spain, aren’t you? · She likes tea, doesn’t she?

p: After a negative statement, the tag is positive.
ex: You aren’t tired, are you? · He didn’t call, did he?

p: Use ‘be’ with ‘be’; with other verbs use do/does/did; with the present perfect use have/has; with modals repeat the modal.
ex: They can swim, can’t they? · You’ve finished, haven’t you?

p: ‘I am’ → tag is aren’t I. ‘Let’s…’ → tag is shall we.
ex: I’m next, aren’t I? · Let’s go, shall we?

grammar.tip: The tag repeats the auxiliary verb and reverses positive/negative. Statement positive → tag negative, and the other way round: ‘He’s here, isn’t he?’ / ‘He isn’t here, is he?’
examples: "You’re a student, aren’t you?"
"She works here, doesn’t she?"
"They didn’t come, did they?"
"He can drive, can’t he?"
"We’ve met before, haven’t we?"
"Let’s have a break, shall we?"

She can swim, can’t she? (positive → negative tag)

reading.title: A Trip to London
reading.text:
Last summer, Daniel and his sister Olivia travelled to London for the first time. They took an early train from Manchester and arrived at about ten o'clock.
First, they visited the British Museum, which was free and very interesting. After that, they had lunch in a small café near the river. In the afternoon, they went on a boat trip and saw many famous buildings.
The weather was warm and sunny all day. In the evening, they were tired but happy. They bought some souvenirs and took lots of photos before they caught the last train home.

reading.text:
My name is Sophie and I'm nineteen. Last year, I got my first job in a small bookshop in Bristol. At first, I was nervous because I didn't have any experience.
My manager, Mr Clarke, was very kind and patient. He showed me how to use the till and how to help customers find books. The other staff were friendly too, so I soon felt comfortable.
I worked part-time, three days a week, and the salary wasn't very high. But I learned a lot, and I really enjoyed talking to customers about books. Now I want to study literature at university.

reading.text:
Hi Grace,

How are you? I'm writing from a small hotel in Brighton, where I've been since Monday. I'm having a wonderful time!

I've already done so many things. I've walked along the beach, eaten fresh fish, and visited the famous pier. Yesterday I went swimming in the sea, although the water was quite cold. I haven't been shopping yet, but I'm planning to go tomorrow.

The weather has been mostly sunny, but it rained a little this morning. The people here are very friendly, and the food is delicious.

I'll be home on Saturday. Let's meet next week — I'll show you my photos!

reading.title: Town or City?
reading.text:
Many people argue about whether it is better to live in a big city or a small town. Both have advantages and disadvantages.
Big cities, like London or Birmingham, are more exciting. There are more jobs, better shops, and lots of things to do in the evening. However, cities are usually more expensive and more crowded, and the air is often more polluted.
Small towns are quieter and cheaper. People are often friendlier and know their neighbours. On the other hand, there are fewer jobs, and young people sometimes find life a little boring.
In my opinion, the best choice depends on your age and your needs. When I was younger, I loved the city, but now I prefer the peace of a small town.

reading.title: The Lost Phone
reading.text:
It was a cold Friday evening, and Emily was hurrying home from work. While she was waiting at the bus stop, she took out her phone to check the time. The bus arrived, and in the rush to get on, she didn't notice that her phone had fallen onto the seat next to her.
When she got home, she realised her phone was missing. She felt terrible — all her photos and messages were on it. She borrowed her flatmate's phone and called her own number, but nobody answered.
The next morning, however, she received an email. A kind passenger named Harry had found the phone and seen her details on the screen. They arranged to meet at a café in the city centre, and Harry returned the phone. Emily was so grateful that she bought him a coffee. Now they are good friends.

grammar.title: Present perfect continuous
grammar.lead: The present perfect continuous links the past to the present and emphasises the duration or repetition of an activity, especially one that is still going on or has only just stopped.
grammar.situation: “You look exhausted!” “Yes, I ’ve been working in the garden all day.” — The present perfect continuous focuses on an activity that has been going on and explains a present result.

p: Use have/has been + verb-ing. It focuses on the activity itself rather than the finished result.
ex: I have been working all day. · She has been studying since nine.

p: Use for + a period and since + a starting point to show how long the activity has lasted.
ex: We’ve been waiting for two hours. · He’s been living here since 2019.

p: The continuous stresses how long / how active; the simple stresses the completed result.
ex: I’ve been reading this book. (still reading) · I’ve read this book. (finished)

p: It can explain a present situation caused by a recent activity.
ex: You look tired. — Yes, I’ve been running.

grammar.tip: Don’t use the continuous with state verbs (know, like, be, have = possess): say ‘I have known her for years’, not ‘I have been knowing’.
examples: "I ’ve been learning English for five years."
"It has been raining all morning."
"They ’ve been working on the project since Monday."
"Why are you so dirty? — I ’ve been gardening."
"She ’s been feeling ill recently."
"We ’ve been waiting for ages."

grammar.title: Past perfect
grammar.lead: The past perfect shows that one past action happened before another past action. It helps to make the order of events in a story clear.
grammar.situation: “When I got to the station, the train had already left.” — The past perfect shows the train left before I arrived. It puts two past events in order.

p: Use had + past participle for the earlier of two past actions.
ex: When I arrived, the train had already left.

p: Often used with the past simple: the past perfect = the earlier action; the past simple = the later one.
ex: She had finished dinner before he came home.

blocks.h: after, before, when, by the time
p: Common with these time linkers to show sequence.
ex: By the time we got there, the film had started.

p: Negative: hadn’t + past participle. Question: Had + subject + past participle?
ex: I hadn’t seen her before. · Had you eaten when they called?

grammar.tip: Use the past perfect only when you need to show one past event happened before another. For a simple sequence (first… then…), the past simple alone is enough.
examples: "When we arrived, the party had already started."
"She had never flown before that day."
"They had finished the work before the boss returned."
"By the time I woke up, he had left."
"I knew I had met him somewhere."
"Had you booked the room before you arrived?"

grammar.title: Future forms
grammar.lead: English uses several forms to talk about the future. Choosing the right one depends on whether you mean a prediction, a plan, an arrangement, a timetable or an instant decision.

p: will = predictions, instant decisions, offers, promises. be going to = plans/intentions and predictions from evidence.
ex: It will snow tonight. · We’re going to paint the house.

p: Use the present continuous for fixed arrangements, usually with a time and another person.
ex: I’m meeting Sara at six. · They’re flying to Rome on Friday.

p: Use the present simple for timetabled events (transport, programmes, schedules).
ex: The train leaves at 9:15. · The film starts at eight.

p: Use may/might for things that are possible but not certain.
ex: It might rain later. · I may go to the party.

grammar.tip: For a plan use ‘going to’; for an arrangement with a time use the present continuous; for a timetable use the present simple; for an instant decision use ‘will’.
examples: "Look at the clouds — it ’s going to rain."
"I think she ’ll pass the exam."
"We ’re having dinner with friends tonight."
"The bus leaves at half past seven."
"I might visit my cousin at the weekend."
"Don’t worry, I ’ll carry that for you."

mistakes.x: The plane will arrive at 6 — it’s the timetable.
mistakes.v: The plane arrives at 6. (timetable → present simple)

mistakes.x: I think I’m passing the exam.
mistakes.v: I think I’ll pass. (prediction → will)
