grammar.title: Second conditional
grammar.lead: The second conditional talks about imaginary, unlikely or unreal present and future situations. It uses the past simple in the if-clause and ‘would’ in the result clause.
grammar.situation: “If I won the lottery, I ’d travel the world.” — The situation is imaginary and unlikely, so we use the past simple + would, not present + will.

blocks.h: Form: if + past simple, would + base
p: The past tense here doesn’t mean past time — it shows the situation is hypothetical.
ex: If I had more money, I would travel.

p: With ‘be’, we often use were for all persons, especially in advice with ‘If I were you’.
ex: If I were you, I’d apologise. · If she were here, she’d help.

p: Use could (ability/possibility) or might (possible result) instead of ‘would’.
ex: If I had a car, I could drive you. · We might win if we tried.

p: First conditional = real/likely; second conditional = unlikely/unreal.
ex: If it rains, I’ll stay in. (likely) · If it snowed in July, I’d be shocked. (unreal)

grammar.tip: For advice, ‘If I were you, I’d…’ is the natural phrase. Don’t mix forms: ‘If I would have money’ is wrong → ‘If I had money, I would…’.
examples: "If I won the lottery, I would buy a house."
"If I were you, I ’d see a doctor."
"She would travel more if she had time."
"If we lived by the sea, we could swim every day."
"What would you do if you lost your job?"
"If he spoke French, he might get the job."

mistakes.x: If I would have money, I would travel.
mistakes.v: If I had money, I would travel. (no “would” after if)

mistakes.x: If I was you, I will help.
mistakes.v: If I were you, I ’d help.

quiz.e: No ‘would’ in the if-clause: If I had money…

o: If I was you, I will help.

grammar.title: Modals of deduction (present)
grammar.lead: We use modal verbs to say how certain we are about a present situation. ‘Must’ shows we are almost sure something is true; ‘can’t’ that it is impossible; ‘might/may/could’ that it is possible.

p: Use must + base verb when you are sure something is true based on evidence.
ex: The light’s on — she must be home.

p: Use can’t (not ‘mustn’t’) when you are sure something is not true.
ex: He can’t be hungry; he’s just eaten.

p: Use these for things that are possible but uncertain.
ex: She might be at work. · They could be lost.

p: Use modal + be + -ing for an action happening now.
ex: He’s not answering — he must be sleeping.

grammar.tip: The opposite of ‘must be’ (sure it is) is ‘can’t be’ (sure it isn’t), not ‘mustn’t be’. ‘Mustn’t’ means prohibition, not deduction.
examples: "You’ve worked all day — you must be tired."
"That can’t be John; he’s in Spain."
"She might know the answer."
"They must be having dinner; the lights are on."
"It could be true, but I’m not sure."
"He can’t be serious!"

mistakes.x: He isn’t home — he mustn’t be at work.
mistakes.v: …he must be at work. (mustn’t ≠ deduction)
She must be working late. (modal + be + -ing)

quiz.q: The lights are on, so she ___ be home.
He's just eaten, so he ___ be hungry.
quiz.e: Sure it’s not true → can’t be.

quiz.q: I'm not sure, but she ___ be at work.

Choose the 'possible' modal.
Find the mistake: 'He's not at home, he mustn't be at work.'
quiz.e: For a likely explanation use ‘must be at work’ (mustn’t is prohibition).

quiz.q: Complete: 'She ___ be ill — she ___ be at the gym; her bag is here.'
quiz.e: ‘might be ill’ (possible) + ‘can’t be at the gym’ (impossible — bag is here).

quiz.q: Which is correct?
Complete: 'No one's answering. They ___ out, or they ___ be sleeping.'
quiz.e: Both uncertain → might be / might be.

quiz.q: Choose the present-continuous deduction.

grammar.title: The passive
grammar.lead: We use the passive when the action is more important than the person who does it, or when we don’t know who did it. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive.
grammar.situation: “This bridge was built in 1890.” — We use the passive when the action matters more than who did it (or we don’t know who did it).

p: Use the right tense of be + the past participle. Present: am/is/are + pp. Past: was/were + pp.
ex: English is spoken here. · The window was broken yesterday.

p: Use by to say who or what does the action, but only when it is important.
ex: The book was written by Orwell. · He was bitten by a dog.

p: Use it when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant, or in formal/scientific writing.
ex: My car was stolen. (we don’t know who) · The results were analysed.

p: Present perfect: has/have been + pp. Future: will be + pp. Modal: can/must be + pp.
ex: The job has been done. · It will be finished soon. · It must be paid today.

grammar.tip: Only verbs with an object (transitive) can be made passive. ‘happen’, ‘arrive’ and ‘sleep’ have no object, so they cannot be passive.
examples: "Millions of phones are made in China."
"The bridge was built in 1890."
"This letter was written by my grandmother."
"The thieves were caught by the police."
"Dinner is being prepared now."
"The work will be finished tomorrow."

mistakes.x: The letter was wrote by John.
mistakes.v: The letter was written by John. (past participle)
The accident happened. (“happen” has no object → no passive)

quiz.e: has/have been + pp: has been done.

quiz.e: will be + pp: will be finished.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'The letter was wrote by John.'

quiz.e: Present perfect passive: has been cleaned.

o: The thief was caught by police.

The thief is catch by police.

quiz.e: Present continuous passive: is being built.

grammar.title: Reported speech: statements
grammar.lead: Reported (indirect) speech tells what someone said without using their exact words. Tenses usually move one step back, and pronouns and time words often change.

p: Move the tense back one step: present simple → past simple; present continuous → past continuous; will → would; can → could.
ex: “I am tired.” → He said he was tired.
“I will call.” → She said she would call.

p: Use tell + a person; use say without a person (or with ‘to’).
ex: She told me she was busy. · She said she was busy.

p: Change pronouns to fit the new speaker, and words like today→that day, tomorrow→the next day, now→then.
ex: “I’ll see you tomorrow.” → He said he’d see me the next day.

p: You can include or leave out that after say/tell.
ex: She said (that) she liked it.

grammar.tip: After tell you must name the listener (tell me/him/us); after say you don’t. ‘He said me’ is wrong → ‘He told me’ or ‘He said’.
examples: "“I’m hungry.” → She said she was hungry."
"“We live in Leeds.” → They said they lived in Leeds."
"“I’ll help you.” → He said he would help me."
"“I can swim.” → She told me she could swim."
"“I’m working now.” → He said he was working then."
"“I bought a car.” → She said she had bought a car."

mistakes.x: He said me that he was late.
mistakes.v: He told me… / He said (that)… (tell + person, say + no person)
She said she would come. (will → would)

"I will call." → She said she ___ call.

Choose the correct verb: 'She ___ me she was busy.'

quiz.q: "I bought a car." → She said she ___ a car.

"I'll see you tomorrow." → He said he'd see me ___.
"I don't like it." → She said she ___ it.

o: She said she finished her homework.
She said she had finished her homework.

quiz.e: present perfect → past perfect: had finished.

quiz.q: Which is correct?
o: He told me he was tired.
He said me he was tired.
He say me he was tired.

o: They said they are leaving now.
They said they were leaving then.
They said they will leave now.

o: He said he can't come tomorrow.

quiz.e: can’t → couldn’t; tomorrow → the next day.

grammar.title: Reported questions & commands
grammar.lead: When we report questions and orders, the structure changes. Reported questions use statement word order, and reported commands use ‘to’ + verb.

p: Keep the question word, then use statement order (subject + verb) with no auxiliary do/does/did.
ex: “Where do you live?” → She asked where I lived.

p: Use if or whether, then statement order.
ex: “Are you ready?” → He asked if I was ready.

p: Use told/asked + person + to + verb. For negatives, use not to.
ex: “Sit down.” → She told me to sit down. · “Don’t move.” → He told me not to move.

p: Reported questions are statements, so they don’t end with a question mark.
ex: He asked where the station was.

grammar.tip: In reported questions, don’t keep the question word order or ‘do/did’: ‘She asked where did I live’ is wrong → ‘She asked where I lived.’
examples: "“What time is it?” → He asked what time it was."
"“Do you like tea?” → She asked if I liked tea."
"“Where are you going?” → He asked where I was going."
"“Close the door.” → She told me to close the door."
"“Please help me.” → He asked me to help him."
"“Don’t be late.” → She told me not to be late."

mistakes.x: She asked me what time was it.
mistakes.v: She asked what time it was. (statement word order)

mistakes.x: He told me to don’t go.
mistakes.v: He told me not to go.

quiz.q: "Where do you live?" → She asked where I ___.
quiz.e: Statement order, backshift: where I lived.

quiz.q: "Are you ready?" → He asked ___ I was ready.
"Sit down." → She told me ___ down.

"Do you like coffee?" → He asked if I ___ coffee.
"Open the window." → She asked me ___ the window.

quiz.e: present cont. → past cont.: was going.

Choose the correct word order.
o: He asked where did I live.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'She asked me what time was it.'
quiz.e: Statement order: what time it was.

o: He asked me not to tell anyone.
He asked me to don't tell anyone.
He asked me don't tell anyone.
He told to not tell anyone.
quiz.e: Negative request → asked me not to tell.

o: She asked if I had finished.

quiz.e: Yes/No + present perfect → if I had finished.

quiz.e: Statement order, backshift: why I was late.

grammar.title: Relative clauses (defining & non-defining)
grammar.lead: Relative clauses add information about a noun. Defining clauses give essential information; non-defining clauses give extra information and are separated by commas.

p: Give essential information (you need it to know which person or thing). Use who, which, that, where, whose. No commas.
ex: The man who lives next door is a doctor.

p: Give extra, non-essential information, set off by commas. Don’t use ‘that’; don’t omit the pronoun.
ex: My brother, who lives in Leeds, is a teacher.

p: In defining clauses, you can omit who/which/that when it is the object.
ex: The book (that) I read was great.

p: whose shows possession; where refers to a place.
ex: She’s the woman whose car was stolen. · That’s the town where I grew up.

grammar.tip: Use commas only for extra information (non-defining). With commas, never use ‘that’ and never drop the pronoun. Without commas (defining), you can use ‘that’ and may drop an object pronoun.
examples: "The keys that were on the table have gone."
"Paris, which is the capital of France, is beautiful."
"The film (that) we saw was boring."
"My uncle, who is a pilot, travels a lot."
"That’s the house where I was born."
"He’s the boy whose dog bit me."

mistakes.x: My car, that is red, is fast.
mistakes.v: My car, which is red, is fast. (non-defining → which)
The man who called… (people → who)

quiz.q: The woman ___ teaches us is very kind.
I bought a phone ___ takes great photos.
That's the café ___ we first met.
She's the girl ___ brother is famous.
Which clause has extra information (needs commas)?
o: The man who called is here.
My dad, who is 60, still works.

quiz.q: In which sentence can we omit the pronoun?
quiz.e: Object pronoun in a defining clause can be dropped: the book I read.

quiz.q: Non-defining: 'London, ___ is the capital, is huge.'
The keys ___ were on the table are gone.
My sister, ___ lives in Bristol, is a nurse.
Choose the defining clause.
o: The man who called is my boss.
Paris, which I love, is busy.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'My car, that is red, is fast.'
Complete: 'The hotel ___ we stayed, ___ was by the sea, was lovely.'
quiz.e: Place ‘where we stayed’ + non-defining ‘which was by the sea’.

quiz.q: Which sentence omits the pronoun correctly?
o: The film we saw was good.

quiz.e: Object pronoun dropped: the film (that) we saw.

quiz.q: Complete: 'He's the player ___ goal won the match, ___ made him famous.'
Choose the correct non-defining sentence.
o: My teacher who is French is kind.

My teacher which is French is kind.

grammar.title: Past habits: used to & would
grammar.lead: To describe the past we can use ‘used to’ and ‘would’ for repeated habits, but only ‘used to’ works for past states. Both contrast the past with the present.

p: used to + base verb describes past habits and past states that are no longer true.
ex: I used to play tennis. · She used to have long hair.

p: would + base verb describes repeated past actions, but not states. It is common in stories.
ex: Every summer we would visit my grandparents.

blocks.h: would vs. used to with states
p: Don’t use ‘would’ with state verbs (be, have, like, know). Use ‘used to’.
ex: ✓ I used to be shy. · ✗ I would be shy.

p: For ‘used to’: didn’t use to / Did … use to? (no -d).
ex: He didn’t use to like coffee. · Did you use to live here?

grammar.tip: Use ‘would’ only for repeated actions. For past states (be, have, like, know), you must use ‘used to’: ‘I used to have a bike’, not ‘I would have a bike’.
examples: "We used to live by the sea."
"On Sundays, my dad would cook a big breakfast."
"She used to be very shy."
"He didn’t use to exercise, but now he runs daily."
"As children, we would play outside all day."
"Did you use to have a dog?"

mistakes.x: I would have a red car when I was young.
mistakes.v: I used to have a red car. (state → used to)

mistakes.x: Did you used to live here?
mistakes.v: Did you use to live here? (after did → no -d)

quiz.q: I ___ play football every day as a child.

quiz.e: ‘would’ can’t be used with the state ‘be’.

___ you use to have a bike?

grammar.title: Gerunds & infinitives
grammar.lead: Many verbs are followed by a gerund (-ing) and others by an infinitive (to + verb). Some verbs take either form, and a few change meaning depending on which you choose.

p: After enjoy, finish, avoid, suggest, mind, keep, practise, can’t stand, look forward to, and after prepositions, use the -ing form.
ex: I enjoy cooking. · She’s good at drawing. · I look forward to seeing you.

p: After want, decide, hope, plan, promise, agree, offer, refuse, manage, learn, would like, use to + verb.
ex: We decided to leave. · He refused to help.

p: Some verbs take an object then to-infinitive: want, ask, tell, allow, advise, expect.
ex: She asked me to wait. · They allowed us to stay.

p: A few verbs change meaning: stop, remember, try, forget.
ex: I stopped smoking. (gave it up) · I stopped to smoke. (paused in order to)

grammar.tip: After prepositions (about, of, at, in, before, after, without), always use the -ing form: ‘I’m interested in learning’, ‘before going out’.
examples: "I can’t stand waiting in queues."
"She decided to study abroad."
"He’s thinking about changing jobs."
"They asked me to help them."
"Remember to lock the door. (don’t forget)"
"I’ll never forget visiting Rome. (the memory)"

mistakes.x: I’m interested in to learn Spanish.
mistakes.v: I’m interested in learning Spanish. (preposition + -ing)
They allowed us to stay.

We decided ___ early.
She's good at ___.
He refused ___ the question.
Do you mind ___ the window?
They asked me ___ them.
I'm thinking about ___ a new car.
She managed ___ the problem.
We're looking forward to ___ you.

o: he paused in order to smoke

quiz.q: Complete: 'I tried ___ the box, but it was locked, so I tried ___ a knife.'

grammar.title: Comparing: as…as, less, modifiers
grammar.lead: Beyond basic comparatives, we can show that two things are equal, that one is inferior, or how big the difference is. These patterns make comparisons more precise.

p: Use as + adjective + as to say two things are the same, and not as … as for inequality.
ex: She’s as tall as her brother. · It’s not as cold as yesterday.

p: Use less + adjective + than (the opposite of ‘more … than’), usually with longer adjectives.
ex: This film is less interesting than the book.

p: Make comparatives stronger or weaker with much, far, a lot, a bit, slightly.
ex: He’s much taller than me. · It’s a bit warmer today.

p: Use ‘the + comparative … the + comparative’ to show that two things change together.
ex: The more you practise, the better you get.

grammar.tip: To strengthen a comparative, use much or far (much/far better), not ‘very’. ‘Very better’ is wrong; ‘much better’ is correct.
examples: "Maths is as difficult as physics for me."
"This phone is not as expensive as that one."
"Today is far hotter than yesterday."
"The book is less exciting than the film."
"He runs a bit faster than me."
"The harder you work, the more you earn."

mistakes.x: This car is very better than mine.
mistakes.v: …is much better than mine. (much/far, not very)

mistakes.x: She is as tall than him.
mistakes.v: She is as tall as him.

Complete: '___ you practise, ___ you become.'

o: She is as tall as him.

A isn't as good as B.

quiz.q: Complete: 'The ___ we leave, the ___ we'll arrive.'
Choose the correctly modified comparative.

grammar.title: Quantifiers
grammar.lead: Quantifiers tell us about amount and number. At B1 we extend beyond some/any to all, most, both, neither, none, each and every, and learn how they combine with nouns and ‘of’.

p: Use these for general amounts. With ‘the/my/these’ + noun, add of: most of the students.
ex: Most people like music. · None of the answers were right.

p: both = the two together; neither = not one and not the other; either = one or the other.
ex: Both films are good. · Neither answer is correct. · Either day is fine.

p: Both mean ‘all, seen individually’, and take a singular verb. ‘every’ for the whole group; ‘each’ for the individuals.
ex: Every student has a book. · Each answer is different.

p: a few + countable, a little + uncountable, several = more than a few (countable).
ex: A few people came. · A little milk. · Several students passed.

grammar.tip: every and each are followed by a singular noun and verb: ‘Every student is here’, not ‘every students are here’.
examples: "Most of my friends live abroad."
"None of the shops were open."
"Both answers are correct."
"Neither of us wants to go."
"Every child needs love."
"Several people complained."

mistakes.v: Every student is present. (every + singular)
Most people are kind. (no “of” without the/my)

___ of the students passed.
___ answers are correct — well done!
___ student has a textbook.

quiz.q: ___ child in the class is different.

quiz.e: More than a few, countable → Several.

quiz.e: every + singular: Every student is present.

quiz.q: Complete: '___ of the two options is fine; choose ___ you like.'
quiz.e: Either of the two is fine; choose either.

grammar.title: Conditionals: zero, first & linkers
grammar.lead: Conditionals describe results that follow from conditions. The zero conditional states facts; the first conditional describes likely future situations. Linkers like unless and as long as add precision.

p: Use if/when + present, present for things that are always true.
ex: If you heat water, it boils.

p: Use if + present, will + base for real, likely future situations.
ex: If it rains, we’ll stay in.

p: unless = if … not. It introduces the only condition that changes the result.
ex: I won’t go unless you come too. (= if you don’t come)

blocks.h: as long as / provided that / in case
p: as long as / provided that = on condition that; in case = as a precaution.
ex: You can stay as long as you’re quiet. · Take an umbrella in case it rains.

grammar.tip: Don’t use ‘will’ after if/unless/as long as/in case in the condition: ‘If it will rain’ is wrong → ‘If it rains, we’ll stay in.’

grammar.title: Articles: a / an / the / zero
grammar.lead: Articles are small but tricky. ‘A/an’ introduces something new or one of many; ‘the’ points to something specific or already known; and we use no article (zero) for general ideas and most plurals/uncountables.

p: Use a/an with singular countable nouns mentioned for the first time or as examples. ‘an’ before a vowel sound.
ex: I saw a dog. · She’s an engineer. · It takes an hour. (silent h)

p: Use the when both speaker and listener know which one, for unique things, and when mentioned again.
ex: The sun is hot. · I bought a book; the book was great.

p: Use no article for plural and uncountable nouns in general, and most names, meals, and many places.
ex: Dogs are loyal. · I like music. · We have lunch at one.

p: Some places take ‘the’ or zero by convention.
ex: go to school/work/bed (zero) · play the piano · in the morning

grammar.tip: Use ‘a/an’ when it’s new or one of many, and ‘the’ when it’s specific or already known. For general statements with plurals/uncountables, use no article: ‘Books are useful’, not ‘The books are useful’.
examples: "She’s a teacher and an artist."
"The Earth goes round the Sun."
"I love coffee in the morning."
"We went to school by bus."
"He plays the guitar very well."
"Children need plenty of sleep."

reading.title: A Change of Career
reading.text:
For ten years, Daniel had worked as an accountant in a busy office in Birmingham. The salary was good, but he had never really enjoyed the job. He often felt bored, and by the end of each week he was exhausted.
Last year, everything changed. While he was helping a friend repair an old house, he realised how much he loved working with his hands. After a few months, he made a brave decision: he resigned from his job and started training as a carpenter.
Now Daniel earns less money than before, but he is much happier. He says he should have changed careers years ago. 'If I had known how good it would feel,' he says, 'I would have done it sooner.'

reading.title: Living Abroad
reading.text:
When Sophie moved from Bristol to Spain, she expected the first few months to be easy. She had visited the country several times on holiday and had always loved the weather and the food. However, living abroad turned out to be very different from visiting.
At first, she found everyday tasks difficult. Simple things, such as opening a bank account or going to the doctor, were stressful because of the language. She often felt lonely and missed her family.
Gradually, things improved. She joined a local Spanish class, where she met other newcomers, and slowly she began to make friends. After a year, she felt completely at home. 'Moving abroad was the hardest thing I have ever done,' she says, 'but also the best.'

reading.title: The Power of Habit
reading.text:
Most of us would like to change something about our lives — to exercise more, eat better, or waste less time. Yet good intentions are rarely enough. Research suggests that the secret to lasting change is not willpower, but habit.
A habit is an action we repeat so often that it becomes automatic. Once a behaviour becomes a habit, we no longer have to think about it or force ourselves to do it. The difficulty, of course, is building the habit in the first place.
Experts recommend starting small. Instead of promising to run for an hour every day, you might begin with just ten minutes. It is also helpful to attach a new habit to an existing one — for example, doing a few exercises straight after brushing your teeth. If you keep the goal small and repeat it daily, it will eventually feel natural.

quiz.e: Attach the new habit to an existing one.

reading.text:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to complain about a jacket I bought from your online shop on 3 May (order number 4471).

When the jacket arrived, I was very disappointed. Although the website described it as dark blue, the jacket I received was clearly black. Furthermore, there was a small hole in one of the pockets, which suggests it had not been checked properly before being sent.

I have been a regular customer for several years and have never had a problem before. However, on this occasion I am not satisfied with the quality of the product or the service.

I would therefore like a full refund. I have attached a photograph of the jacket as evidence. I look forward to hearing from you within seven days.

Yours faithfully,
J. Harris

reading.title: The Interview
reading.text:
Emily had prepared for weeks. She had researched the company, practised her answers, and chosen her clothes carefully the night before. By the time the morning arrived, she felt ready — or so she thought.
The trouble began on the way there. Her train was cancelled, and by the time she found another, she was already running late. When she finally reached the office in Manchester, she was twenty minutes behind and out of breath.
To her surprise, the manager was understanding. He explained that one of his own interviews, years earlier, had gone badly for similar reasons, and he had still been offered the job. The interview went well, and Emily relaxed.
A week later, an email arrived. She had got the job. Looking back, she realised that the disaster on the way had actually helped: it had shown the manager how she behaved under pressure.

grammar.title: Third conditional
grammar.lead: The third conditional talks about unreal situations in the past — things that did not happen — and their imagined results. We use it to express regret, criticism or relief about the past.
grammar.situation: “If I had studied medicine, I would have become a doctor.” — But I didn’t study medicine, so I’m not a doctor. The third conditional imagines a different past.

blocks.h: Form: if + past perfect, would have + past participle
p: Both clauses refer to an imagined past that is now impossible to change.
ex: If I had studied, I would have passed.

p: Use could have (ability/possibility) or might have (possible result) instead of ‘would have’.
ex: If we’d left earlier, we could have caught the train. · She might have won if she’d tried.

p: ‘I’d’ can mean ‘I had’ or ‘I would’. In the if-clause it is ‘had’; in the result it is ‘would’.
ex: If I’d known (had), I’d have told you (would).

p: Express regret, criticism, or relief about a finished situation.
ex: If you’d listened, this wouldn’t have happened.

grammar.tip: Never use ‘would have’ in the if-clause: ‘If I would have known’ is wrong → ‘If I had known, I would have…’.
examples: "If I had known, I would have helped."
"She would have passed if she had revised."
"If we’d left earlier, we could have caught the bus."
"They might have won if they had played better."
"If it hadn’t rained, we would have gone out."
"You wouldn’t have got lost if you’d used a map."

grammar.title: Mixed conditionals
grammar.lead: Mixed conditionals combine two time frames. The most common type links a past condition to a present result, or a present condition to a past result.

p: if + past perfect, would + base. A past action affects the present.
ex: If I had taken the job, I would be rich now.

p: if + past simple, would have + past participle. A present (general) fact affects the past.
ex: If I were more careful, I wouldn’t have made that mistake.

p: Words like now, today, still often signal a present result from a past cause.
ex: If she hadn’t missed the flight, she would be here now.

p: Mixed conditionals are unreal in both clauses; only the time frames differ.
ex: If I spoke French (now), I would have understood them (then).

grammar.tip: Decide the time of each clause separately: if the cause is past, use past perfect; if the result is present, use ‘would + base’ (not ‘would have’).
examples: "If I had saved money, I would be on holiday now."
"If she were taller, she would have joined the team."
"If we hadn’t moved, we would still live in Leeds."
"If he weren’t so shy, he would have spoken to her."
"If I had learnt to drive, life would be easier now."
"If you liked sport, you would have come with us."

grammar.title: Wish & if only
grammar.lead: We use ‘wish’ and ‘if only’ to talk about things we would like to be different. The tense we choose shows whether we mean the present, the past, or an annoying situation we want to change.

p: For present situations we want to be different, use the past simple (or ‘were’).
ex: I wish I had more time. · I wish I were taller.

p: For regrets about the past, use the past perfect.
ex: I wish I had studied harder.

p: For another person’s annoying behaviour, or a change we want, use would.
ex: I wish you would stop shouting. · I wish it would stop raining.

p: if only works like ‘wish’ but is more emphatic.
ex: If only I hadn’t said that!

grammar.tip: Don’t use ‘wish + would’ about yourself. Say ‘I wish I could…’, not ‘I wish I would…’. Use ‘would’ for other people’s behaviour.
examples: "I wish I knew the answer."
"I wish I hadn’t eaten so much."
"I wish you would listen to me."
"If only I were on holiday now."
"She wishes she had taken the job."
"If only it would stop snowing!"

grammar.title: The passive: advanced
grammar.lead: At B2 we use the passive across all tenses and in impersonal reporting structures, which are common in news and academic writing to report opinions without naming a source.
grammar.situation: “The painting is thought to be a fake.” / “It is said that he is very rich.” — Impersonal passive structures report opinions without naming who says them.

p: Form the passive with the correct tense of be + past participle, including perfect and continuous forms.
ex: The road is being repaired. · The work had been finished. · It will have been done.

p: Use It + is/was + reporting verb + that… to report general opinions.
ex: It is said that he is very rich. · It was believed that the Earth was flat.

p: A second pattern: Subject + is/was + said/thought + to + infinitive.
ex: He is said to be rich. · She is thought to have left the country.

p: Use have/get + object + past participle when someone does a service for you (see causatives).
ex: I had my car repaired.

grammar.tip: In ‘He is said to have left’, use the perfect infinitive (to have + pp) when the action is earlier than the reporting.
examples: "The bridge is being rebuilt at the moment."
"The results had been announced before we arrived."
"It is believed that prices will rise."
"The painting is thought to be a fake."
"He is said to have made a fortune."
"The decision will have been made by Friday."

grammar.title: Reported speech: reporting verbs
grammar.lead: Beyond ‘say’ and ‘tell’, English uses many reporting verbs that summarise the function of what was said — such as offer, promise, suggest, admit and refuse — each with its own grammar pattern.

p: offer, promise, agree, refuse, threaten, decide.
ex: He offered to help. · She refused to answer.

p: advise, ask, tell, warn, remind, encourage, invite.
ex: They advised me to wait. · He warned us not to go.

p: suggest, admit, deny, recommend, mention.
ex: She suggested leaving early. · He admitted breaking it.

p: apologise for, insist on, accuse sb of, congratulate sb on.
ex: He apologised for being late. · She insisted on paying.

grammar.tip: Match the verb to its pattern: ‘suggest’ takes -ing or ‘that…’, never ‘to’. ‘He suggested to go’ is wrong → ‘He suggested going’.
examples: "She offered to drive me home."
"They warned us not to swim there."
"He admitted stealing the money."
"I apologised for forgetting her birthday."
"The doctor advised him to rest."
"She insisted on seeing the manager."

mistakes.x: She suggested to meet at six.
mistakes.v: She suggested meeting at six. (suggest + -ing)
He apologised for being late.

She suggested ___ a taxi.

quiz.e: warn + object + not to: not to stay.

grammar.title: Past modals of deduction
grammar.lead: To make guesses about the past, we use a modal verb + have + past participle. These show how certain we are that something happened, based on present evidence.

p: Use must have + past participle when you are sure something happened.
ex: The ground is wet — it must have rained.

p: Use can’t/couldn’t have + pp when you are sure it did not happen.
ex: He can’t have finished already; it’s too soon.

p: Use these for things that possibly happened but you’re not sure.
ex: She might have missed the bus. · They could have got lost.

p: Use should have + pp for the right thing that didn’t happen (regret or criticism).
ex: You should have told me. · I shouldn’t have eaten so much.

grammar.tip: For deduction the opposite of ‘must have’ is ‘can’t have’, not ‘mustn’t have’. ‘Mustn’t have’ is not used for deduction in standard English.
examples: "The lights are off — they must have gone out."
"She can’t have seen us; she didn’t wave."
"He might have forgotten the meeting."
"You should have called a doctor."
"I shouldn’t have said that."
"They could have taken the wrong road."

mistakes.x: He mustn’t have heard the bell.
mistakes.v: He can’t have heard the bell. (negative deduction → can’t have)
You should have called me.

quiz.e: Sure it happened → must have rained.

Complete: 'She passed easily — the exam ___ very hard.'
quiz.e: Sure it wasn't hard → can't have been.

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.e: should have + past participle: should have called.

grammar.title: Relative clauses: advanced
grammar.lead: At B2 we use more formal relative structures: prepositions before the relative pronoun, ‘whose’ for possession, and quantifiers like ‘some of whom’ and ‘both of which’ in non-defining clauses.

p: In formal English the preposition can go before the relative pronoun (which/whom).
ex: The man to whom I spoke… · The house in which they live…

p: In everyday English we usually move the preposition to the end and may drop the pronoun.
ex: The man (who) I spoke to… · The house (that) they live in…

p: In non-defining clauses use all/some/many/none/both + of whom/which.
ex: I have three sisters, all of whom are doctors.

p: whose shows possession for people and things.
ex: A company whose products are famous… · The author, whose books I love…

grammar.tip: After a preposition use whom (not ‘who’) and which (not ‘that’): ‘the person to whom…’, ‘the tool with which…’. ‘To that’ and ‘to who’ are wrong here.
examples: "The colleague with whom I work is brilliant."
"This is the book about which we spoke."
"She has many friends, most of whom live abroad."
"They sell phones, none of which are cheap."
"He’s an artist whose work sells worldwide."
"The reason for which he left is unclear."

mistakes.x: The client to that I wrote replied.
mistakes.v: …to whom I wrote… (preposition + whom)

mistakes.x: I have two cousins, both of who are nurses.
mistakes.v: …both of whom are nurses.

quiz.e: born in a house → in which.

Choose the correct 'whose' sentence.
o: The painter who paintings sell well is here.

grammar.title: Causative: have/get something done
grammar.lead: We use the causative when we arrange for someone else to do a service for us, rather than doing it ourselves. The structure focuses on the result, not on who does the work.
grammar.situation: “I don’t cut my own hair — I have it cut.” — The causative shows that someone does a service for you. The focus is on the result, not who does the work.

p: The standard structure: have + thing + past participle.
ex: I had my hair cut. · We had the house painted.

p: get is a more informal alternative to ‘have’.
ex: I got my car repaired. · She got her photo taken.

p: Change the tense of ‘have/get’ as needed.
ex: I’m having my eyes tested tomorrow. · He’s had his phone fixed.

p: The same structure can describe something bad that happened to you.
ex: She had her bag stolen. · They had their flight cancelled.

grammar.tip: The order is have + OBJECT + past participle, not ‘have + past participle + object’. Say ‘I had my car washed’, not ‘I had washed my car’ (that means you did it yourself).
examples: "I had my suit cleaned for the wedding."
"We’re getting the kitchen redecorated."
"He had his tooth taken out."
"She got her hair coloured."
"They had their car broken into."
"I need to have my passport renewed."

mistakes.x: I had repaired my bike at the shop.
mistakes.v: I had my bike repaired. (have + object + past participle)
I’ll have the roof fixed.

quiz.e: Causative past: had my hair cut.

quiz.e: had + object + past participle: had it cancelled.

o: I'll have fixed the roof for me.
quiz.e: have + object + past participle: have the roof fixed.

grammar.title: Gerunds & infinitives: advanced
grammar.lead: Some verbs are followed by either a gerund or an infinitive, but with a clear change of meaning. Knowing the difference lets you say exactly what you mean.

p: + to = the duty comes after; + -ing = the memory comes before.
ex: Remember to lock the door. (do it) · I remember locking it. (memory)

p: stop + -ing = end the activity; stop + to = pause in order to do something.
ex: He stopped smoking. (quit) · He stopped to smoke. (paused)

p: try + -ing = experiment; try + to = attempt something difficult.
ex: Try adding salt. (experiment) · I tried to open it. (attempt)

p: regret + -ing = be sorry about the past; regret + to = be sorry to announce. mean + -ing = involve; mean + to = intend.
ex: I regret saying it. · I regret to inform you… · This job means travelling. · I meant to call.

grammar.tip: With ‘remember/forget’: use the infinitive for a task you must do, and the -ing form for a memory of something already done.
examples: "Please remember to post the letter."
"I’ll never forget meeting her."
"He stopped to rest for a minute."
"Try turning it off and on again."
"I regret to tell you the news is bad."
"Studying abroad means leaving home."

mistakes.x: I regret to tell him the truth; now he’s angry.
mistakes.v: I regret telling him… (regret + -ing = sorry about the past)

mistakes.x: On the walk we stopped taking photos. (meaning: paused to take)
mistakes.v: …we stopped to take photos. (pause in order to)

quiz.q: Remember ___ the door when you leave.
I remember ___ him at the party last year.

On the walk, we stopped ___ photos.
quiz.e: Paused in order to → to take.

quiz.e: Sorry to announce → regret to say.

quiz.q: The recipe didn't work. Try ___ more sugar.

quiz.e: Attempt at something hard → tried to open.

quiz.q: This new job means ___ to another city.
I'm sorry, I meant ___ you earlier.
Don't forget ___ your medicine tonight.
Find the mistake: 'I regret to tell him the truth; now he's angry.'
quiz.e: Sorry about the past → regret telling.

quiz.q: Complete: 'I'll never forget ___ the Pyramids, but please remember ___ the tickets.'
Which means 'he paused his walk to make a call'?
quiz.e: stop + to = pause in order to.

quiz.q: Complete: 'We regret ___ you that the flight ___, so we tried ___ another route.'
o: to inform / has been cancelled / to find
quiz.e: regret to inform + passive + tried to find.

quiz.q: Choose the correct pair.
o: Remember posting it (do it now) / I stopped to smoke (quit).
Remember to post it (do it) / I stopped smoking (quit).
Remember to post it / I stopped to smoke means I quit.

grammar.title: Future perfect & continuous
grammar.lead: To talk about the future in detail, we use the future continuous for actions in progress at a future time, and the future perfect for actions that will be completed before a future point.

p: An action that will be in progress at a specific future time.
ex: This time tomorrow I will be flying to Rome.

blocks.h: Future perfect: will have + past participle
p: An action that will be finished before a future time, often with ‘by’.
ex: By 2030 they will have built the bridge.

p: Use by + time or by the time + clause with the future perfect.
ex: By the time you arrive, I will have left.

p: will have been + -ing stresses the duration up to a future point.
ex: By June I will have been working here for ten years.

grammar.tip: Use the future continuous for something happening at a future moment, and the future perfect for something completed before that moment.
examples: "At 8 pm I ’ll be having dinner."
"By Friday we ’ll have finished the report."
"This time next week she ’ll be lying on a beach."
"By the time he’s 30, he ’ll have travelled the world."
"In May I ’ll have been studying here for three years."
"Don’t call at six — I’ll be driving."

mistakes.x: By next month I will finish the course.
mistakes.v: By next month I will have finished… (completed before → future perfect)

mistakes.x: Don’t call at six — I will drive.
mistakes.v: …I’ll be driving. (in progress → future continuous)

quiz.q: This time tomorrow I ___ to Spain.
quiz.e: In progress at a future time → will be flying.

quiz.q: By next year, they ___ the new road.
quiz.e: Completed before a future time → will have built.

quiz.q: At 9 pm tonight, we ___ the match.
By the time you arrive, I ___.

quiz.e: Completed by a deadline → will have finished.

quiz.q: This time next week, they ___ on holiday.

quiz.e: Duration up to a future point → will have been working.

quiz.q: By 2040, scientists ___ a cure, perhaps.
Choose the action in progress at a future time.
Find the mistake: 'By next month I will finish the course.'
quiz.e: Completed before a future time → will have finished.

quiz.q: Complete: 'At noon we ___ the test; by 2 pm we ___ it.'
o: will be taking / will have finished
will have taken / will be finishing
quiz.e: In progress ‘will be taking’ + completed ‘will have finished’.

quiz.q: Which stresses duration up to a future point?
o: By May I'll have been writing for a year.

quiz.q: Complete: 'By the time the film ends, we ___ here for three hours.'
quiz.e: Duration up to a point → will have been sitting.

quiz.q: Choose the correct future perfect.
quiz.e: will have + past participle: will have left.

grammar.title: Past perfect continuous
grammar.lead: The past perfect continuous shows that an activity had been in progress for a period before another point in the past. It emphasises duration and often explains a past situation.
grammar.situation: “She had been waiting for an hour when the bus finally came.” — The past perfect continuous shows how long an activity had gone on up to a past moment.

p: Use had been + verb-ing for an action that continued up to a point in the past.
ex: She had been waiting for an hour when the bus came.

p: It often explains why something was the case at a past moment.
ex: His eyes were red because he had been crying.

p: Use for + period and since + starting point.
ex: They had been living there for years before they moved.

p: The continuous stresses the activity/duration; the simple stresses the completed result.
ex: I had been reading. (activity) · I had read the book. (finished)

grammar.tip: Don’t use the continuous with state verbs. Say ‘I had known her for years’, not ‘I had been knowing’.
examples: "He was tired because he had been working all night."
"We had been driving for hours when the car broke down."
"She had been studying French before she moved to Paris."
"The ground was wet; it had been raining."
"They had been arguing before we arrived."
"I had been waiting for ages when she finally called."

mistakes.x: I had been knowing him for years before he left.
mistakes.v: I had known him for years… (state verb → simple)

mistakes.x: They had been lived there for years.
mistakes.v: They had been living there for years.

quiz.q: She ___ for an hour when the bus arrived.
quiz.e: Duration up to a past point → had been waiting.

quiz.q: His eyes were red because he ___.
quiz.e: Explains the past result → had been crying.

quiz.q: They ___ for hours before they stopped.
The form of the past perfect continuous is ___.
It was wet outside; it ___.
We ___ for the train when it was cancelled.
quiz.e: Duration before a past event → had been waiting.

quiz.q: She was out of breath because she ___.
quiz.e: Explains the state → had been running.

quiz.q: How long ___ they ___ before they got married?
Which verb is WRONG in this form?
Choose the duration form.
o: I had been reading for hours.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'I had been knowing him for years before he left.'
Complete: 'By the time help arrived, they ___ for three hours.'
quiz.e: Duration up to a past point → had been swimming.

quiz.q: Which stresses the completed result?
o: She had been painting the room.
She had been paint the room.
quiz.e: Completed → past perfect simple: had painted.

quiz.q: Complete: 'He failed because he ___ instead of revising.'
quiz.e: Ongoing activity explaining the result → had been playing.

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: They had been lived there for years.
They had been living there for years.

They had living there for years.

grammar.title: Inversion
grammar.lead: In formal or emphatic English, certain negative or limiting adverbials at the start of a sentence force inversion — the auxiliary verb comes before the subject, as in a question.
grammar.situation: “Never have I seen such a mess.” — In formal or emphatic English, a negative word at the start pushes the auxiliary in front of the subject, like a question.

p: After never, rarely, seldom, hardly, no sooner, not only, little at the start, invert subject and auxiliary.
ex: Never have I seen such a mess. · Rarely does she complain.

p: Used for one event quickly following another.
ex: Hardly had we arrived when it started to rain. · No sooner had he spoken than she left.

p: Not only + auxiliary + subject, … but also …
ex: Not only did he apologise, but he also paid.

p: After only then / only after / only when / not until, invert.
ex: Only when she left did I realise. · Not until midnight did they finish.

grammar.tip: Inversion uses the same auxiliary you’d use in a question: ‘Never have I…’, ‘Rarely does he…’, ‘Not only did she…’. Don’t use normal word order after these openers.
examples: "Never have I been so embarrassed."
"Rarely do we see such talent."
"Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang."
"No sooner had they left than it snowed."
"Not only is she clever, but she’s kind too."
"Only after the test did he relax."

mistakes.x: Never I have eaten such good food.
mistakes.v: Never have I eaten such good food. (invert: aux + subject)

mistakes.x: Not only she sings, but she dances.
mistakes.v: Not only does she sing, but she also dances.

mistakes.x: No sooner he had left when it rained.
mistakes.v: No sooner had he left than it rained.

quiz.e: No sooner had he opened … than.

quiz.q: Which is correct?
o: Not only she sings, but she dances.

quiz.e: Not only does she sing, but she also dances.

quiz.q: Complete: 'Only after he left ___ how rude he had been.'
quiz.e: Inversion after ‘Only after’: did I realise.

quiz.q: Rewrite with inversion: 'I had rarely felt so happy.'
o: Rarely I had felt so happy.
Rarely had I felt so happy.

quiz.e: Rarely had I felt so happy.

grammar.title: Cleft sentences
grammar.lead: Cleft (‘divided’) sentences split one idea into two clauses to emphasise a particular part. They are very common in speech for adding focus and contrast.

p: Emphasise a person, thing, time or place.
ex: It was Tom who broke it. · It was in 2010 that we met.

p: Emphasise the whole idea, often an action or need.
ex: What I need is a holiday. · What he did was (to) call the police.

blocks.h: The thing / the reason / the place
p: Other openers add focus too.
ex: The reason (why) I’m late is the traffic. · The place where we stayed was lovely.

p: All can mean ‘the only thing’.
ex: All I want is peace and quiet.

grammar.tip: In a What-cleft, the verb ‘be’ is singular even before a plural idea if ‘what’ is the subject: ‘What I need is answers’ (not ‘are’).
examples: "It was my sister who called, not me."
"It’s your help that I need."
"What surprised me was his honesty."
"What we did was book another flight."
"The reason I left was the noise."
"All she wanted was the truth."

mistakes.v: What I want is answers. (“what” as subject → singular verb)

mistakes.x: It was John which sent the email.
mistakes.v: It was John who sent the email.

quiz.q: ___ Tom who broke the window.

___ I want is some peace.
It was Sarah ___ helped me.
What he did ___ apologise.

It's not the money ___ matters.
What surprised everyone ___ his decision.
Choose the cleft emphasising the place.
o: We stayed in a lovely hotel.
It was the hotel that we loved.

quiz.e: The place where… = focus on place.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'What I want are answers.'
Rewrite to emphasise 'John': 'John sent the email.'
o: It was John who sent the email.
It was the email who John sent.

quiz.e: It was John who sent the email.

quiz.q: Complete: '___ we should do ___ tell the truth.'
quiz.e: What we should do is tell the truth.

quiz.q: Which correctly emphasises the reason?
o: The reason why he left was the noise.
The reason what he left was the noise.
It was the reason the noise left.

quiz.e: The reason why he left was the noise.

quiz.q: Complete: '___ that I admire ___ her honesty.'
quiz.e: The thing that I admire is her honesty.

grammar.title: Linking & contrast
grammar.lead: Linkers of contrast and concession join ideas that seem to conflict. The right choice depends on whether the linker is followed by a noun, an -ing form, or a full clause.

p: Followed by a subject + verb.
ex: Although it was late, we kept working. · Even though she tried, she failed.

p: Followed by a noun or -ing form, not a clause. Add ‘the fact that’ to use a clause.
ex: Despite the rain, we went out. · In spite of being tired, he worked. · Despite the fact that it rained…

p: Link two sentences; usually start a new sentence with a comma after.
ex: It was expensive. However, we bought it.

p: Show a direct contrast between two ideas.
ex: He likes tea, whereas she prefers coffee.

grammar.tip: Use ‘although’ before a clause and ‘despite / in spite of’ before a noun or -ing. ‘Despite it was raining’ is wrong → ‘Despite the rain’ or ‘Although it was raining’.
examples: "Although he was rich, he wasn’t happy."
"Despite the traffic, we arrived on time."
"In spite of feeling ill, she came."
"The plan was risky. Nevertheless, it worked."
"I love cities, whereas my brother prefers the countryside."
"Even though it costs more, it’s worth it."

mistakes.x: Despite it was cold, we swam.
mistakes.v: Although it was cold… / Despite the cold… (despite + noun, not a clause)

mistakes.x: Although it was hard but he tried.
mistakes.v: Although it was hard, he tried. (no “but” with although)

quiz.q: ___ it was raining, we went out.
___ the rain, we went out.
He likes coffee, ___ she prefers tea.
It was expensive. ___, we bought it.
In spite ___ the cost, they travelled.
___ being tired, she finished the race.
___ he studied hard, he didn't pass.
Choose the linker + clause.

quiz.e: Despite + noun/-ing; before a clause use ‘Although’.

quiz.q: Complete: '___ his wealth, he was unhappy, ___ his brother, who had little, was content.'
Which is correct?
o: In spite the danger, they climbed.

reading.title: The Remote Working Debate
reading.text:
Since the pandemic, working from home has become normal for millions of people. Supporters argue that it offers a better work-life balance: employees save hours that would otherwise be wasted commuting, and many report feeling less stressed and more productive.
Not everyone is convinced, however. Some managers worry that staff who work remotely are harder to supervise and less connected to their colleagues. Younger workers, in particular, may miss the informal learning that happens in an office, where they can pick up skills simply by watching experienced people.
The truth probably lies somewhere in between. A growing number of companies in Manchester and London now offer a 'hybrid' model, in which employees spend part of the week at home and part in the office. Had this option been available ten years ago, it might have seemed strange. Today, it is increasingly seen as the best of both worlds.

reading.title: Living with Artificial Intelligence
reading.text:
Artificial intelligence is no longer science fiction. It already recommends the films we watch, filters our emails, and helps doctors read medical scans. For many, these developments are exciting; for others, they are a cause for concern.
Those who welcome AI point to its potential to save lives and time. A computer can examine thousands of images far faster than a human, spotting patterns that might otherwise be missed. In industries from farming to finance, AI is helping people make better decisions.
Yet the same technology raises difficult questions. If a self-driving car causes an accident, who is responsible? As machines take over more tasks, some jobs will certainly disappear. Supporters argue that new jobs will be created, just as they were during the Industrial Revolution. Critics are less sure. What seems clear is that AI is here to stay, and societies will need to decide carefully how to use it.

reading.title: Why We Put Things Off
reading.text:
Almost everyone procrastinates. We delay important tasks, choosing instead to check our phones, tidy a drawer, or make yet another cup of tea. We know we are wasting time, and yet we do it anyway. Why?
Psychologists suggest that procrastination is not really about laziness. It is more often about emotion. When a task makes us feel anxious or bored, our brain looks for an escape, and a quick, pleasant distraction provides instant relief. The problem, of course, is that the relief never lasts, and the task only grows more stressful.
The good news is that procrastination can be managed. Experts recommend breaking a large task into small steps, so that it feels less frightening. It also helps to forgive yourself for past delays; research has shown that students who stopped criticising themselves actually procrastinated less in future. In other words, being kinder to ourselves may be the first step towards getting things done.

reading.title: Report: Improving the Town Library
reading.text:
Introduction
The purpose of this report is to assess the current state of Brighton Central Library and to recommend improvements. The findings are based on a survey of 200 users and interviews with staff.

Findings
The majority of users praised the library's wide selection of books. However, several problems were identified. Firstly, the opening hours were felt to be too limited, particularly for those who work full-time. Secondly, the building's Wi-Fi was described as slow and unreliable. Finally, a number of younger visitors complained that there was nowhere quiet to study.

Recommendations
In light of these findings, it is recommended that the library extend its opening hours into the evening. Furthermore, the Wi-Fi system should be upgraded as a priority. Were a quiet study area to be created on the upper floor, it would almost certainly attract more students.

Conclusion
With relatively modest investment, the library could serve the community far more effectively.

reading.title: The Cost of Cheap Travel
reading.text:
Never before has travel been so affordable. Budget airlines now offer flights across Europe for the price of a meal, and millions of us take advantage every year. Yet this golden age of cheap travel comes at a price that does not appear on the ticket.
The most obvious cost is environmental. Aviation produces a significant share of carbon emissions, and a single long flight can undo months of careful recycling. Less visible, but no less serious, is the impact on popular destinations. Cities such as Venice and Barcelona have become so crowded with visitors that local residents are being pushed out of their own neighbourhoods.
None of this means we should stop travelling altogether. Travel broadens the mind and supports countless livelihoods. What it does suggest is that we should travel more thoughtfully — flying less often, staying longer, and respecting the places we visit. Only if tourists and governments act together will the benefits of travel be preserved for future generations.

listening.script: Good morning, everyone. Today we're looking at the psychology of decision-making. Now, we like to think we make choices logically, weighing up the facts. But research suggests otherwise. In fact, most of our decisions are driven by emotion and by mental shortcuts the brain uses to save effort. These shortcuts are usually helpful, but they can lead to predictable mistakes. For example, people tend to fear losing something far more than they value gaining the same thing. This is called loss aversion, and we'll explore it in detail after the break. For now, I'd like you to read chapter four before next week's seminar.

grammar.title: Inversion for emphasis
grammar.lead: Advanced English uses inversion — putting the auxiliary before the subject — to add drama and formality. It is common in writing, speeches, and formal speaking.

leadTr.uz: Ilg'or ingliz tilida urg'u berish uchun inversiya ishlatiladi — yordamchi fe'l egadan oldin keladi. Bu yozma nutq va rasmiy uslubda ko'p uchraydi.
leadTr.ru: В продвинутом английском для усиления используется инверсия — вспомогательный глагол ставится перед подлежащим. Это характерно для письменной и формальной речи.

p: After never, rarely, seldom, little, no sooner, not only — invert subject and auxiliary.
ex: Never have I seen such dedication.
Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.

p: Had / Should / Were can replace 'if' in formal conditionals.
ex: Had I known, I would have called.
Should you need anything, ask.

p: So + adjective and Such + noun phrase can open the sentence with inversion.
ex: So intense was the storm that flights stopped.
Such was the noise that nobody slept.

grammar.tip: Inversion is a spice, not a staple — one per paragraph is plenty.
examples: Rarely does a film capture a book so well.
Little did they know what awaited them.
No sooner had we arrived than it started to rain.

grammar.title: Cleft sentences
grammar.lead: Cleft sentences (It was… that…, What I need is…) split one message into two clauses to control emphasis — a hallmark of fluent, natural English.

leadTr.uz: Cleft gaplar (It was… that…, What I need is…) bitta fikrni ikki qismga bo'lib, urg'uni boshqaradi — bu ravon ingliz tilining belgisi.
leadTr.ru: Расщеплённые предложения (It was… that…, What I need is…) делят одну мысль на две части, управляя акцентом — признак свободного владения языком.

p: Emphasise who, what, when or where with It + be + focus + that/who.
ex: It was Maria who solved it.
It was in 2019 that everything changed.

p: What + clause + be + focus emphasises the thing itself.
ex: What I need is a long holiday.
What annoyed me was the silence afterwards.

p: All + clause + be + focus means 'the only thing'.
ex: All I asked for was five minutes.
All it takes is practice.

grammar.tip: In speech, wh-clefts buy you thinking time while sounding sophisticated.
examples: It's the small details that matter.
What makes her different is her patience.
All we can do is wait.

mistakes.x: It was Maria which solved it.
mistakes.v: Use who for people: It was Maria who solved it.

mistakes.x: What I need it is a holiday.
mistakes.v: No extra pronoun: What I need is a holiday.

quiz.q: ___ the ending that ruined the film for me.
What impressed the panel ___ her honesty.
quiz.e: Wh-cleft takes singular be: What impressed them was…

quiz.q: ___ I'm saying is that we need more time.
quiz.e: What I'm saying is… — emphasising the message.

quiz.q: It was only when I reread the letter ___ I understood.
quiz.e: It-cleft closes with that: …that I understood.

grammar.title: The subjunctive & formal structures
grammar.lead: Formal English preserves the subjunctive after verbs like suggest, demand, insist — and fixed phrases like 'be that as it may'. Mastering it lifts your writing register instantly.

leadTr.uz: Rasmiy ingliz tilida suggest, demand, insist kabi fe'llardan keyin subjunktiv saqlanadi. Uni egallash yozuv uslubingizni darhol ko'taradi.
leadTr.ru: Формальный английский сохраняет сослагательное наклонение после глаголов suggest, demand, insist. Владение им сразу повышает регистр письма.

p: After suggest/recommend/demand/insist + that, use the base form for all persons.
ex: They insisted that she be present.
We recommend that he take the earlier train.

p: Some subjunctives survive only in set expressions.
ex: Be that as it may…
Suffice it to say…
Far be it from me to judge.

p: Use 'were' for all persons in hypotheticals.
ex: If I were in your position…
I wish it were simpler.

grammar.tip: In American English the mandative subjunctive is standard; British English often uses 'should' instead — both are correct.
examples: The board demanded that the report be rewritten.
It is essential that every voice be heard.
If he were honest, he'd admit it.

mistakes.v: Base form after suggest: …that he go home.

mistakes.x: If I was you, I'd wait.
mistakes.v: Hypothetical: If I were you, I'd wait.

quiz.e: It is vital that + base form: …that she be informed.

quiz.e: Wish + were-subjunctive: I wish it were possible.
